subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REFLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, January 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Yves Leduc (Verdun) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REFLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many will agree that in the policy of the throne speech there has been a noticeable trend towards saying less of future plans and of dwelling more on past achievements. This policy is all right for government members because they have ready-made for them a speech which can be dressed up with some slight detail; but for a member of the opposition who wants to do a conscientious job, it is not all right. He is forced to take a negative approach to the throne speech itself and consequently he falls back on this negative method of regretting that no action has been taken or of regretting that the wrong action has been taken. At the beginning of my speech I wish to apologize for this negative approach but with this trend apparent in the speech from the throne, I cannot see how any different attitude can be taken.
In the maritimes generally and in Saint John in particular we find the same situation prevailing, that of loss of markets, and unemployment. I think I should be fair and generous to say that the grain shipments through Saint John have increased somewhat, but unemployment is, at the best, about the same as it was last year. But there is a dangerous trend, Mr. Speaker, towards an increase in welfare demands. To me that means that the unemployment of past years is catching up with us. I know that in Saint John this Christmas the welfare demands of the citizens were four and five times as great as those of the previous year. There is a danger that should be noted there. In approaching this important throne speech
The Address-Mr. Bell debate in a constructive way, we find in the speech only vague references to regional and seasonal unemployment. There is mention of the commonwealth conference which is of interest to us, but nothing more is said. I am pleased that our amendment lists the loss of markets and the unemployment situation first in that order.
I have a long list of these so-called regrets but in picking out four or five I first would say that we regret the further loss of the United Kingdom markets. This hackneyed phrase of putting all our eggs in the one trade basket has perhaps been worn a little bit thin but one is forced to comment that it must be some basket by now.
The figures on the United Kingdom market show that in the first nine months of 1954- and they are the only figures readily available-British imports from Canada dropped in value to $192 million from $228 million in the same period last year. What is more noteworthy is that this decline in Canadian sales to the United Kingdom came at a time when other United Kingdom imports remained constant. In other words, the United Kingdom has held its own with imports from other countries-South Africa, India, New Zealand, Ceylon and so on-but their imports from Canada decreased sharply to the amount that I have shown.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) goes to the commonwealth conference with his contingent, surely it is not too much to ask that for the first time we take a little bit of leadership with regard to these interesting trade problems. If it is necessary to take the leadership in the matter of convertibility, in some limited way, let us do that. If it is a matter of some imperial preference, let us not be afraid to examine this matter and to push for it at the conference. I had occasion to do some research work on preferences and tariffs, and it amazed me to note that in the past history of imperial preferences, all leadership has been taken by the members of the commonwealth or of the empire, as it was then. There has never been any definite stand or a definite forcing of opinion by the so-called mother country in these matters. I feel strongly that we should not hesitate to take a strong stand in these two matters of convertibility and preferences.
Also interesting in this connection were the statements made last year by Mr. Thomas McKittrick, who appeared before the trade relations committee of the other place, when he made the bland remark that convertibility was in the hands of Canada. That is a statement by one of the leading bankers of the United States, and he was throwing on our

The Address-Mr. Bell shoulders the responsibility of bringing Britain and the United States together. This surely would be a great time for us to show that leadership which we so obviously have been hesitant to take.
We also regret the increasing trend to ship Canadian produce and manufactured goods through United States ports. I have here some figures that show that there has been little decrease in the amount of produce that is being sent to the other ports of the world from Canada through the United States. The figures are still alarming and no definite trend can be indicated. The figures that are more alarming perhaps are the ones that show our protected industries-that is industries in Canada which have some degree of protection -are the ones that use these United States ports almost exclusively. The figures are as follows:

These figures are of great concern to us because Canada has invested thousands of dollars in her transport facilities and yet we have not followed through with encouragement of domestic and foreign trade. It is a well known fact that the United States government is continually encouraging and advertising the use of their ports, but we seem to have fallen down in that respect. We have comparable facilities at our Canadian ports. Our handling is efficient, costs are supposed to be on a parity with United States rates, and yet when our ports need definite help because of economic conditions such help is not forthcoming. The government should take some definite action. It has not only a responsibility but also a definite obligation to see that these industries which are protected to a great extent should be forced in some manner to use Canadian ports for both import and export trade.
There has been considerable interest by Canadian manufacturers but the time has come when the government will have to give consideration to taking some action in this regard. One suggestion that should be investigated is the possibility of having our trade commissioners authorized and instructed that in their negotiations in other countries regarding imports and exports they should 
solicit the use of Canadian ports entirely. The United States government does it. Why can we not do the same thing?
We further regret that no action has been taken on the request of the provincial government of New Brunswick with respect to hydroelectric development. The other day Mr. James Muir, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, said at the bank's annual meeting that there must be a farsighted policy to develop Canada's resources. We in New Brunswick are proud of the fact that this year we are spending $182 million on capital investment. This exceeds the figure for 1954 and is a new high, representing an increase of almost $18 million over the previous year's total of $164 million. On a percentage basis these figures indicate that our province is ahead of all other provinces in capital investment. Surely that is a good indication that we want to help ourselves. We have been able to dig up enough money on our own to lead the country.
The St. Lawrence seaway is taking shape and progressing. The pipe line is moving ahead, although I would not wish to comment on the present position of progress in this respect. But when these all-Canadian developments are presented to us we wonder why our request for hydroelectric development cannot be considered in the same way. It was interesting to note the other day that Mr. Rand Matheson of the maritime transportation commission made the first noteworthy statement that I have seen on the effect of the seaway on the maritime ports. He is reported as saying that, as business is taken inland with the development of the seaway, manufacturers and other exporters will tend to ship more during the summer months and thus decrease the winter business of the maritime ports.
This situation is alarming to us and we wonder why consideration cannot be given to our appeals. This is an appeal made in a non-partisan way. The opposition members of the New Brunswick legislature have given some sort of approval. At least they have not objected. To my knowledge no New Brunswick member in the House of Commons has raised any objection. Their silence is a little bit alarming to me although the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) did comment on it the other day, and there is a non-partisan approach to the whole matter.
More hydroelectric power would solve our industrial bottleneck and we could make plans for the development of our new mineral discoveries. It amused me very much

to read in a newspaper the other day that Canada was permitting $3 million of its Colombo plan money to be used for hydroelectric development in India. It is quite ironical when you think that we in New Brunswick are asking for assistance with respect to our hydroelectric power development and cannot seem to get anywhere. Yet it is all right for the Canadian government to give $3 million to India to develop hydroelectric power there. This necessary assistance would enable us to round out our development. It would go a long way to help our economy. Of course there is the fact that the Atlantic provinces comprise a regional market of nearly two million people. In the years ahead Canadian industries in the central part of Canada would for various reasons such as high freight rates perhaps wish to decentralize their industries by coming to the maritimes. We would be able to offer them hydroelectric power and the regional market that is available. Surely we are not going to get a no answer to this request.
In the third place we regret that in the changes and reorganization of the reserve army that took place during the past summer there was gross discrimination against us. I should like to review the story briefly so far as New Brunswick is concerned, and also Nova Scotia to some extent. We have always prided ourselves on the high number of our enlistments. In the first and second world wars I think we had the highest per capita enlistment of any of the provinces of Canada. We have a background of good training and tradition in our provinces, particularly in my own province with which I am a bit more familiar.
Last year I put a question on the order paper asking the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) the present state, classification and training position of all the reserve army units in Canada. To my mind this was the key question as far as the changes were concerned and how they should be effected. The question went to the head of the order paper, stayed there for two months and that was the end of it. I suggest that these figures would have uncovered the unmistakable fact that our New Brunswick units were in A-one shape and probably unsurpassed anywhere in Canada. What happened? When the changes were made last year our three regiments, the North Shore regiment, the Carleton and York regiment and the New Brunswick Scottish, were wiped out entirely. It was not a case of reduction or reorganization, to which we might not have had any objection. It was simply the fact that in New Brunswick and 50433-19
The Address-Mr. Bell Nova Scotia the units, as such, were completely wiped out. These are the only provinces in Canada in which the new units were given a provincial designation. When the major-generals Letson, Kennedy and Renault came down to New Brunswick to investigate the matter, they were only there for two hours. They talked to one or two army officials and gave no indication that these changes were coming. Evidently they went away without a clear picture of the facts.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that we do not object to the changes that had to be made. We realize that some reorganization of the reserve army had to take place. We do object to the fact that our units were completely wiped out. In reply to letters that were sent, the minister said it was necessary to reduce the infantry and increase the armour. I ask the question today, where is the increase in armour in the regiments in New Brunswick? There has not been any change whatever. Again there is a touch of irony in this whole case, as was the case in my previous regret. One regiment is now to be called the First New Brunswick Regiment, so we are right back where we started in 1793 because there was a Royal New Brunswick Regiment at that time.
We regret also, Mr. Speaker, the discontinuance of the railway lines in Albert county. There is a history connected with these lines that goes back a long way. The first reference in any act is to the Elgin line. This railway was originally partly financed by the people in the area surrounding Elgin. They were forced to buy bonds to help with this railway. When the Canadian National took it over, certain statements were made and a definite obligation was undertaken to continue this line which is so necessary to the residents of that area. The cheese factory at Elgin, the lumber and pit prop business as well as the new mineral discoveries, particularly copper in this area, all need this line of railway. The highways will not take the heavy load that the railway line can accommodate, so it is an absolute necessity that further consideration be given to any plans that are in the minds of the transport commission or the railway to tear up those tracks.
Another point of interest concerns the recent discoveries in Albert county, particularly of oil shale. New Brunswick has invested considerable money in a complete examination of the possibility of burning oil shale to provide electric power. A new New York firm has been approached and is in the process of doing that. I suggest it would be folly to do away with these railway
290	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Bell lines while the future looks so bright. While this was taking place, and while considerable opposition was building up to the loss of this line, evidently the government, in their sly little way, were toying with the idea of eliminating a further line in Albert county, the Hillsborough to Albert line. Just the other day the residents in this area were notified that there is to be a board hearing to ascertain why this line should not be removed.
One goes back twenty years when there was some talk of removing the same line, but for some reason or other the government left it there. Later gypsum was discovered and it was possible to locate quite a profitable industry in the area. If this line had been abandoned the industry, of course, could not have been accommodated. Here we are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars to develop the marshlands in Albert county in a successful way for the future, and at the same time talk of removing the railway line. What is going to happen to this investment in the marshlands? We sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government, through the Canadian National, will give every consideration to these appeals that the lines be left in their present position.
We regret further that there is too much rigidity in the Post Office Department around our area. Good officials are hamstrung because of the rigid requirements imposed by Ottawa. They make investigations quite thoroughly with respect to changes in the post office and carrier service, yet they are bound by the rigid requirements of the Post Office Department. The local officials fall back on the Ottawa department and their excuses, consequently bad public relations exist. Personally, I can say that I have had quite a few inquiries of the Post Office Department and I must admit that prompt replies have been received. There seems to have been a betterment of the condition that was. so criticized during the last session.
However, in the East Saint John area the people greatly desire a new post office. The surrounding district of Little River feels it is entitled to a sub-post office. The Glen Falls area has been petitioning for some time for rural mail service. I understand that all these requests have gone through the local department in the proper way and have received the approval of the local officials. Someone here at Ottawa or back in Saint John has fallen back on the rigid requirements of the department that so much has to be given for a mail contract or a box has to be within so many yards of here or there before this mail service can be inaugurated.


I suggest that some little discretionary power given to the local officials would not be out of the way in helping to repair the bad public relations that are building up.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to develop the pattern that seems to be shaping up in our area, particularly with reference to this debate. There has been this reckless abandonment of rail lines in Albert county, which seems to be contrary to the enthusiasm engendered by our new discoveries; there has been this indiscriminate undermining of our traditions, traditions that only we in the maritimes really appreciate, and we do object quite seriously to this discrimination against our army units. Personally I feel that the rail lines would not have been removed nor the army units changed if they were in the central areas which have more powerful lobby groups to speak for them. Little Albert county is out of the way. Changes can be made there without too much objection.
In so far as the army units are concerned, we do not have the powerful officers' messes of the Queen's Own or the Black Watch that could lobby with influential men. We feel that our regiments mean just as much as these other units, and we object very strongly to these two changes merely because of the effect politically. However, I must say in all fairness, Mr. Speaker, that it is significant to know that the loss of markets which has been affecting us for the last two or three years is now touching the whole dominion. I feel certain that when everybody becomes aroused over the matter it will help us. I feel certain also that we will not be turned down in our pleas for assistance in connection with hydroelectric power, particularly in the light of the news that India is to get some help.
There is a new interest in the maritimes, perhaps for the first time in recent years, with our discoveries. A new spirit seems to be developing. We feel now that by standing in unity we may be able to make use of the lessons we have learned in the past. It is gratifying to note the success of the Atlantic economic council that is meeting regularly now each year. This was the dream of the late Premier Angus L. Macdonald, and I am sure his spirit will always be alive while that council is meeting.
I had occasion this past summer to make some general remarks on maritime union, and I must say for the record that I have never said anything rightly or wrongly that caused as much interest as this subject. I did not receive a word from anyone who was opposed to it; in fact everyone who spoke offered comments of a complimentary nature.

It may be far removed, but surely any steps we can take in this respect will benefit all of us.
I was also very much pleased the other day to hear the hon. member from Halifax (Mr. Balcom) speak about the need for regional assistance in a financial way in the maritime provinces. I believe his observations were to the effect that the maritimes have a continuing problem, and that a regional agency should be set up along the lines of the industrial development bank. In any event, it is just another way of saying that we do need collective help down there, and I compliment him upon his remarks in this respect.
We have had very clear indications of the government's interest in our fishing problem, and it is encouraging to know that our fisheries-perhaps one of Canada's most undeveloped industries-are being given some help, and that research is continuing in this respect.
These last few words perhaps paint a little brighter picture than those with which I began, when I mentioned those things I thought it necessary to point out. But I do feel that perhaps the government has finally begun to take note of our traditions. We have finally got our backs up and we are going to do a little fighting for some of our new discoveries. I believe that when we see on a wall or in print the motto of Canada, which was offered by a father of confederation from New Brunswick, we will not have to blush any more, because perhaps Canada will really be a nation from sea to sea.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REFLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first to add my congratulations to those which' have already been extended to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, upon the exceedingly able manner in which they discharged their duties. It is reassuring to the membership of the house when these more recent additions bring with them the capacity for clear thinking and lucid expression, indicating a full sense of their responsibility as members of this Canadian parliament. I add my congratulations most heartily to those which have already been given to them.
Then, with regard to the speech from the throne itself, as we always do, we have heard hon. members expressing a wide diversity of opinion concerning the value of the government's program which has been set out in that speech. Let me say that in my opinion the speech from the throne is a source of justifiable satisfaction to supporters of the government. When one reads it and 50433-194
The Address-Mr. Lusby hears it, and when one sees the measures there promulgated, he realizes that it reveals and outlines a program for the session now beginning which is well timed and, while perhaps not spectacular, represents a steady advance for improvements which lead always to the greater welfare of the Canadian people.
Nothing has emanated from the opposition benches to cause me to doubt the correctness of the opinion I have just expressed. We have heard of course the cry, which is so easily uttered by those who do not have to shoulder any responsibility, for lighter taxes and heavier expenditures. We have heard broached again-or at least hinted-the ancient and, I believe, the now thoroughly exploded doctrine that high and higher tariff walls are the panacea for all our ills.
Then, from more than one source we have heard what seems to me in effect to be a complaint that it is not good that the Liberal party should have at its head a man of such high character and outstanding ability as our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and that we Liberals should not take such great pride in that fact. That position, of course, is understandable from the opposition's point of view.
Then we have listened to a very considerable amount of what I have no doubt would be deemed suitable stump material in certain quarters of the country, such as the prophecy commented upon so much in the latter part of the debate as to the possible coming victory of the communists in Quebec and the socialists everywhere else. All I have to say concerning that prophecy is that it is a very well balanced one, because I think one-half of it is just as likely to be fulfilled as the other.
We have heard presented the hoary and inevitable argument that no matter what beneficial measures the government may see fit to introduce, it should have gone farther and provided a little more. But, of sound and constructive criticism-and, after all, that is or should be the chief aim of opposition par-it seems to me that there has been a distinct paucity. And I think this very lack is in itself a not inconsiderable tribute to the strength of the government's policies.
No thinking man will suggest, of course, that everything is exactly as we should like to see it. In Canada, as everywhere else in the world, inevitably there are certain problems, some of which are national and some regional, some of which are minor and others more important, which inevitably must be faced and, if possible, overcome.
Speaking as one from the maritime provinces let me say that in that section of the
292	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Lusby country we always have a full share of regional problems. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell), who is also from the maritime provinces, has just concluded a speech in which quite properly he laid a great deal of emphasis upon the regional problems of the maritimes. I should like to say something along similar lines, although of course my approach will be different from his, and will seek to emphasize more the problems of my own constituency. For at the mention of regional problems we think of those with which the maritime provinces have to contend. And one thing that stands out is this, that as each year rolls around we see and the world sees unmistakably that Canada as a nation is advancing into a glorious future. Not all the talk from the opposition benches can seriously impugn the truth of that statement. But it is also unfortunately true that not all parts of the country are advancing at the same pace. We in the maritime provinces are advancing, yes, but not at the same pace as is enjoyed by others parts of the country. In the maritimes we lack a central geographical position; we lack vast hinterlands and, to a considerable degree, untouched natural resources. And when I say that, of course I have in mind the fact that great discoveries of mineral resources have been made in New Brunswick and to some extent in Nova Scotia.
Nevertheless we do lack to a very considerable degree untouched natural resources. We have a lack of easy access to profitable markets. These are conditions of geography, conditions due to our situation. Nevertheless they militate against us.
I think it is correct to say that every province of Canada, with the exception of the maritimes, enjoys some, and certain of them enjoy all, of the advantages which I have said we lack. Therefore, as equal partners in the great scheme of confederation, of which two of the maritime provinces are charter members, we are legitimately entitled to claim special consideration from the federal government with respect to the problems which we have to face, to the end that in the advancement of this country-I refer particularly to economic advancement, for in other respects socially, culturally and intellectually, we can hold our own without difficulty-to the end, I repeat, that in the economic advancement of this country we in the maritimes shall have our place, if not in the vanguard at least within hailing distance of the more fortunate provinces.
I do not mean by that and I do not suggest that in a country of this size there can be absolute equality in this respect in all regions.


For example, I do not suggest that Nova Scotia can foreseeably hope to match in this particular, let us say, the province of Alberta where, if I might use a figure of speech, we might say that the good ship prosperity rides snugly, perhaps even smugly, in a sea of oil. I suppose some hon. gentlemen might suggest that I carry that figure of speech a little further and put Social Credit in the role of a stowaway.
But I do say that much can be done and every possible step should be taken to alleviate existing economic inequalities. This government can perform no greater service in the interests of Canada as a whole, not merely in the interests of the maritimes, than to bend its energies and turn its resources toward the accomplishment of that end. A few days ago during the course of this debate one of the hon. members for Halifax suggested the possibility of close liaison between some federal agency and the newly formed economic council of the Atlantic provinces, and also suggested the desirability of encouraging new industry in the maritimes by the greater use of the facilities of the industrial development bank. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) mentioned that just a few moments ago. I heartily endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax in that respect. I should like to add my compliments to those which have been tendered the hon. member by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert.
It seems to me, as the hon. member for Halifax indicated, that in the past the efforts made to improve the economic life of the maritimes have been of too sporadic and piecemeal a character, involving perhaps the appointment of a temporary commission to consider some problem when it has become acute, but never a continuous program of research and investigation which would permanently carry on and cover all phases of the maritime economy. I should like to see the creation or appointment of some permanent federal body charged with such duties, acting of course in the closest co-operation with all organizations in the maritimes having the same purposes in view, including the newly formed economic council of the Atlantic provinces.
In a developing and changing country such as this, with its vast distances and great diversity of interests, it is not surprising that steps may need to be taken from time to time to ensure that adequate attention shall be given to the needs of a particular area. Perhaps I may cite as an example-I do not think it is too good a one-the fact that last year it was found desirable to effect a change

in the name of the former department of resources and development which has now become the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, marking the reorientation of the work of that department with increasing emphasis upon the administration of the northern territories.
Although this analogy is not by any means a perfect one, I use it to stress the desirability, I think I might say the necessity, of providing some effective mechanism whereby the economic problems of the maritimes can be kept in a constant focus of attention by this government and means for their solution devised, not sporadically but as a part of a comprehensive program to raise the whole economy of these provinces to a level more nearly commensurate with that enjoyed elsewhere in Canada. One of the primary points of such a program would most certainly be the promotion of greater industrial activity in the maritimes where factors which I have already mentioned militate heavily against us in that respect.
In this connection let me revert to the speech from the throne and say that, of the beneficial measures thereby adumbrated, the proposed increase in unemployment benefits, already partly put into effect, has perhaps aroused the most general public interest and approval. Certainly this is true of industrial centres such as my own town of Amherst. This measure to my mind marks a further expansion of that sweeping program of social security instituted by the Liberal party and still proceeding as the continuing development and increasing wealth of the country permit. Yet, and here at last I find some common ground with opposition speakers, unemployment insurance, beneficial though it has proved, is certainly no complete answer to any problem of unemployment which may arise. Obviously the only real and complete answer is a continued high level of industrial activity.
I am very far from agreeing with the belief, or apparent belief, of some of the opposition members that the federal government, singlehanded, or any other government for that matter, by a sort of waving of the wand of its magical powers, so to speak, can permanently end unemployment. But I do suggest as one ameliorating policy, which at least to some extent lies within its powers, that the federal government, rather than promoting the further undue concentration of secondary industries in those parts of the country which are already highly industrialized, should turn its efforts toward increasing the level of industrial activity in the maritimes.
This of course is not by any means a new proposition. It has frequently been broached
The Address-Mr. Lusby that this wider distribution of industry is desirable. I think it is usually approached from the point of view that in the event of war it would be a good thing in the interests of national safety and defence. But I think, taken in the perspective of years, it would also prove a strong weapon in preventing or combating unemployment.
In this free land the government cannot say to one industrialist "Build there" and to another "Build here." I never have a great deal of sympathy for those who say that the government should build an industry in that town or this town. Under our present system that is not the right approach to the problem. But we must remember that in these days the federal government exerts a very weighty and potent influence upon the industrial life of our country. It is a mighty buyer, a mighty awarder of contracts. I urge that some suitable scheme of regional allocation of these contracts should be devised which would promote the further industrialization of the maritime provinces. I say further that it is in the national interest that this should be done.
Turning again to the speech from the throne, I, like other hon. members, am deeply interested in the proposal for an expanded program of public works. As I have mentioned before in this house, I consider the most desirable type of public works, those most to be encouraged, to be not those which only furnish employment during the stage of construction, or which may be a mere matter of pride or convenience to residents of a community or district, but those which may reasonably be expected to provide a permanent stimulus to the whole regional economy.
Such are the Canso causeway and the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry, and such will be the Chignecto canal project when that long overdue project is finally undertaken. Surely in the light of present developments, in the light of the St. Lawrence seaway, the iron ore development in Labrador, maritime security in time of war and the expressed intention of the government to embark upon an expanded program of public works, no time could be more opportune for instituting a new, thorough and conclusive investigation into the feasibility and economic possibilities of this canal. At this date it is not germane to say that a commission which conducted a survey in 1931 decided against the commercial value of the canal. Conditions now are in no way similar to those of 25 years ago. I think the whole subject should be approached anew. A commission

The Address-Mr. Lusby should be appointed and a thorough investigation made, taking into account representations from all interested areas. A final decision should then be taken as to whether the Chignecto canal is to be built.
We in the maritimes firmly believe the decision would be a favourable one, but I think I may say that if, after a thorough investigation of the matter, it was decided that the canal could not be commercially justified, then the people of the maritimes would be content to accept that decision. But they are not content to allow this matter to stand year after year without any further reinvestigation into the merits of the canal.
Another badly needed project which I should like to bring to the attention of the government is the establishment of a ferry service across Minas channel between Parrs-boro in my constituency and the opposite shore in Kings county. I should say the reestablishment of a ferry service; for prior to its discontinuance during the last war such a service had, I am told, been in existence in one form or another for over a century, although I suppose it was originally a sailing ship proposition.
However, it is a rather stark commentary that in this year of progress, after such a long period, no such ferry operates. The provision of adequate deep water docking facilities near Parrsboro and cape Blomidon on the far shore would enable a ferry service to be maintained over a few miles of water and independently of the tides. Such facilities would eliminate an overland journey of some 150 miles. Such a ferry would, as a glance at the map of Nova Scotia and the maritimes will demonstrate, greatly expedite traffic between western Nova Scotia on the one hand and Cumberland county, Prince Edward Island, and the north shore of New Brunswick on the other. It would certainly provide a substantial impetus to the Nova Scotia tourist trade, and I believe in many ways it would be complementary to the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry service which is shortly to go into effect.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in this modern age any worth-while improvement in transportation facilities such as I have suggested should merit the careful consideration of the federal government. Indeed, the federal government has an interest in transportation in many ways, not least of which is its interest and support of the building of the trans-Canada highway. Therefore, without reservation, I would urge this government to carry out a new and comprehensive investigation of the Chignecto canal project, and ask them to provide full co-operation
rMr. Lusby.]

and assistance in the establishment of the Minas channel ferry service which I have mentioned.
Another public works project of a different character which I also strongly commend to the attention of this government is the erection of a new armoury in the town of Spring-hill which is in my constituency. For years the existing armoury in that sturdy mining community of some 8,000 people, an ancient wooden structure, not erected by the government in the first place, has been inadequate for its purposes. Now it has been officially condemned as unfit for use. No renovation or reconstruction will prove a satisfactory substitute for a new and modern building.
In this connection let me add that if a community's record of patriotism and military service is to be taken into account in such a case, the town of Springhill is entitled to very high priority indeed. In both great wars the percentage of enlistments from the town was among the highest in Canada, and in the two wars 140 Springhill men fell in the armed service of their country. I would add that enlistment figures were very high in spite of the fact that a great many miners were held at their work in the mines under wartime regulations.
In peacetime reserve army activities are maintained at a high level in the town, with approximately 100 men on the strength oi the local company and training each week. Future interest in matters military is ensured by an efficient and enthusiastic cadet corps which has held the best standing in military district No. 6 on various occasions, and in 1950 and 1952 won the King George trophy for marksmanship-emblematic of the Canadian championship. We need not doubt that if the need again arises the rugged miners of Springhill will pour to war as valiantly as in the past.
These are things to be taken into account when consideration is being given to our request for the construction of a new armoury. The present lack of a suitable armoury is a serious handicap to military training and a damper on enthusiasm. We should also bear in mind the importance of a suitable armoury as a meeting place in the social, sporting, and public life of the community.
In this respect I would like to say a few words about the reorganization of militia units in the maritimes. Reorganization took place in Nova Scotia and it was with deep regret that we learned that the honourable name of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders could not be maintained, and that a military unit could not be known as such. The North Nova Scotia Highlanders had a very high

and honourable tradition in the last war, and much as we regret that the need for efficiency and economy has meant the disbanding of the unit, I do not believe it will affect the interest and enthusiasm for military training in that area. That being the case, I say that Springhill is fully deserving of a new armoury and I urge the government to provide one as soon as possible.
While on the subject of public works I should like to recommend a comprehensive survey of the docking, dredging, and other harbour and channel requirements of the various ports along the two coast lines of my constituency, Wallace, Pugwash, Northport, Advocate, Spencer's Island, Port Greville, Parrsboro, and the rest. Fishing and Shipping are still important constituents in the economy of Cumberland county and deserve every reasonable encouragement.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the mention of Springhill, a coal mining town, calls to mind a topic on which I wish to say a few words, for it constitutes what is perhaps the most serious problem in the Nova Scotia economic picture today, that of the coal mining industry.
A great deal has been said in the past in this house about the state of the coal mining industry, but I make no apology for mentioning the subject again. As we enter another year the future of the industry remains generally sombre and cloudy, particularly for the small independent producer. According to the latest report of the dominion coal board, the forecast is very much the same as before, namely that in spite of increasing competition from oil and natural gas, the increase of population and expansion of industry in Canada will provide, or is expected to provide, sufficient markets by the middle sixties to enable the industry to survive, at least at its present level. This forecast, of course, does not take into account the present incalculable factor of atomic power. However, from that forecast I think we may reasonably hope that the industry is not necessarily doomed to extinction for lack of markets. But the next decade will be a critical one. It will require a continued flow of governmental assistance and co-operation to enable the industry to stagger through to better days. Not only in the interest of the coal-producing provinces but in the national interest as well, it is imperative that this assistance and co-operation be continued and, if necessary, expanded. We have only to remember that coal is still the chief source of energy in Canada, that it is still an essential in time of war and that the mines, if they are once closed, will in all probability never reopen.
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy
I am confident that this government will continue to play a full and generous part in the struggle to save the industry, as it has done in the past. What form of assistance may prove most effective is not an easy question to answer, even for experts. It may prove to lie in the realm of the development of new and commercially practicable uses for coal other than as fuel. That has always been a favourite thesis of my own. It may be found elsewhere. The ultimate answer will probably be a composite of many factors. I hope at a later stage of this session to be able to discuss the matter of the coal industry in much greater detail even as I hope to be able to present the needs of the farmers and of other important economic groups in my constituency. But for the present I merely wish to urge upon this house the emergent nature of the situation confronting the coal mining industry and the necessity of finding a satisfactory solution.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I just wish to revert to an earlier stage of my address and to use that example to emphasize again the need for a special degree of attention by this government to the economic problems of the maritimes.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Lusby), who has just taken his seat, on the excellent balance which he maintained in his speech. He spent about two minutes in chastising the opposition groups for their failure to recognize the fact that we have the best of all possible governments today and about thirty minutes telling us of the injustices from which his part of the country is suffering under that same government.
Unlike many Liberals who have spoken, Mr. Speaker, I find nothing in the throne speech on which I can congratulate the government. One hon. member-I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott)-stated that he was doubly thrilled by this speech. Personally I find myself chilled rather than thrilled-
