speechtext:
-by the nonchalant manner in which the grave and serious social and economic problems of this country are completely ignored in the speech from the throne which is now before us. For instance, there is evidence that for the next five or six months we shall be amending and consolidating existing legislation. In the speech from the throne there is nothing to indicate that we are to be presented with any new legislation designed to cope with the problems that face us today. For instance, there is to

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy be no new legislation providing national health insurance, the need for which is growing and for which there is increasing national support. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we are probably expecting too much from this government if we expect them to introduce any such measure as that at a time when we are two or three years from a federal election.
There is to be no improvement in old age pensions, no improvement in family allowances, nor any new social security measures that will redistribute the wealth that we are producing and increase the diminishing purchasing power of the Canadian consumers. No new measures are forecast to check the diminishing net income of our rural population. At a time when bold, progressive measures-measures such as those proposed by this government in their green book of 1945-are needed to meet an unemployment situation which is annually growing more serious, we have offered us nothing that can by any stretch of even Liberal imagination cope with the situation.
It is true that at long last the government has yielded to the repeated requests of veterans organizations and to the annual bombardment from the opposition benches. After nation-wide protest the government has agreed to increase veterans allowances. To the veterans of the country they are offering a few crumbs from a rich uncle's table. There is to be no new housing legislation of such a nature as will make the securing of homes possible for tens of thousands of people who really need homes and who cannot afford to buy them under our present housing legislation, or to rent them. There are no new measures whereby these people may be able to secure houses, unless perchance the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) may be close enough to the government to know what the government's intentions are but which intentions are not expressed in the speech from the throne. If, as I hope, the speech which he made in the house the other day- and which I may say re-echoed requests made by this group a year ago that purchasers' equity in homes should be safeguarded just as is safeguarded the interest of the lending institutions-indicates that there is a prospect of the government's introducing such legislation this year but which they did not forecast in the throne speech, then we say that we are extremely happy. We certainly are delighted to have that speech from the hon. member for Spadina, a member so closely associated with the cabinet that his name on numerous occasions has been mentioned in connection with the post of cabinet minister and other positions within the gift of the government; and I want to

add my voice in support of that suggestion.
I think the Liberal party is missing a grand opportunity, in so far as Toronto is concerned, in having failed to provide some such position for the hon. member for Spadina. Personally, I should like to see him elevated to the Senate. We might then make more progress in Spadina. However, Mr. Speaker, we hope that some such legislation on housing will be introduced.
There are facing the country today many other problems for which no provision is made in the speech from the throne. For instance, we find no provision made for the employable unemployed other than the possible extension of unemployment insurance benefits. Notwithstanding the fact again that in 1945 the government placed itself on record and outlined its policy as being one of providing unemployment assistance for those who failed to benefit from the Unemployment Insurance Act, there is no evidence that we are to have any application of that policy in this session. We are told in the speech from the throne that our national economy is in a generally healthy condition and although there are half a million or more Canadians looking for jobs that are unavailable the matter is dismissed in the speech from the throne in these words:
Some unemployment of a regional and seasonal nature Is being experienced.
Just how healthy is our national economy, and what are some of the danger signals that can be observed today and which we should be observing if we want to keep that economy in a healthy condition? In the first place, Mr. Speaker, it is quite evident that our national production is declining while at the same time our labour force is increasing and our technological processes are being improved to the extent that it is becoming possible to produce more goods with fewer workers every year.
Probably one of the best indicators of the level of our production is provided by the dominion bureau of statistics report on railway carloadings for the first ten months of 1954. These months are compared with the first ten months of 1953, and we find that there is considerable indication that the volume of production in at least 15 major products dropped. These major products include fertilizers, petroleum and petroleum products, pulpwood, lumber, grain products, building products, livestock, logs and posts, merchandise, automobiles, trucks and parts, primary iron and steel, iron ore, farm machinery, machinery and castings, and grain. In all of these there has been a considerable reduction in carload loadings in the first ten months of 1954 compared with

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy
the same months in 1953. The percentage decreases range as follows: For automobiles a drop of 18 per cent, for primary iron and steel a drop of 21 per cent, for iron ore a drop of 23 per cent, for farm machinery 24 per cent, for machinery and castings 25 per cent, and for grain 34 per cent.
The dominion bureau of statistics report on employment in certain basic industries tells much the same story. It tells the story that with unemployment growing in these basic industries to such an extent there must of necessity be a drop in production. The dominion bureau of statistics figures in their report on employment by industries indicate that in the nine month period from January to September, 1954, unemployment increased in all our major goods producing industries. It increased by 11 per cent in clothing and 11 per cent in the railroad equipment industry. In the latter industry unemployment in September, 1954, was 20 per cent higher than in September, 1953.
There is an 11 per cent increase in unemployment in the automobile and parts industry, an increase of 17 per cent in textiles, 17 per cent in primary iron and steel, and 20 per cent in farm machinery. In the case of farm machinery the decline in employment over the comparable period in 1952 was 34 per cent. In the consumer durable goods industries we have, for example, in the first six months of 1954 a decline of 6 per cent in the production of refrigerators and 20 per cent in the production of washing machines. There was a drop of 16 per cent in employment in aircraft plants below the peak of employment in the spring of 1953, and a drop of 14 per cent in employment in shipbuilding between April and September, 1954.
When figures are available for the last three months of 1954 there is no doubt in the world but that they will show that there has been a greater increase in unemployment and a greater drop in production over the entire year than that shown by the figures for the first nine months of the year. The figures pertaining to railway carloadings and unemployment indicate a considerable decline in production in all our major goods industries, particularly in industrial machinery, farm machinery, railroad equipment, aircraft, shipbuilding and consumer durable goods.
A second danger signal that I think we should watch, and which should lead us to the conclusion that our economy is not in that healthy condition that the government would have us believe it is, is the drop in net farm income. As has already been pointed out in the house, 1954 was the third successive year 50433-20
in which net farm income dropped substantially. While official figures are not yet available, it has been unofficially estimated that net farm income for 1954 will show a drop of $400 million. This would mean that between 1951 and 1954, a period of only three years, net farm income has dropped from $2,150 million to $1,200 million, a drop of 44 per cent.
I think we should all realize, Mr. Speaker, that a drop in farm income has of course been the main reason for the depression in farm machinery plants, for the decline in the demand for trucks, for the dropping off of railway traffic and consequently the large unemployment in the railway equipment industry, building materials, fertilizers, fuels, etc. The relationship with respect to the drop in farm income is reflected in the drop in retail sales in the three prairie provinces which are most affected by that drop in farm income. Retail sales in Manitoba, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, in the first nine months of 1954, dropped by 3 per cent, 7 per cent and 12 per cent respectively. I believe that drop in retail sales indicates the extent to which those provinces were hit by the drop in farm income.
A third danger signal to which we should be paying some attention is our export position. Our export position was anything but good in 1954. Sales abroad of Canadian wheat and coarse grains from January through October were down 40 per cent from the same period in 1953. Total merchandise exports in the first ten months of the year dropped off 8 per cent in value as compared with the same period in 1953.
There are also some danger signals, Mr. Speaker, indicating that a decrease in production and employment may continue, in fact is most likely to continue in 1955. We all realize that in a country such as Canada where our labour force is increasing at the rate of something over 60,000 annually, and where technological improvements are being introduced continuously, it is not good enough that our production, and consequently our national income, should remain even at the peaks which they attained in earlier years. It is essential, if we are to keep Canada prosperous, that our national income continue to increase.
Some people find considerable solace in the fact that in the recession year of 1954 wages and salaries were maintained at a comparatively high level. As a matter of fact, wages and salaries improved by 1 - 8 per cent in that year. But the two dynamic factors to which I have referred, that of an increasing labour

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy force and improved technological processes, render it necessary that wages and salary must keep pace with these other two factors. These two factors render the creation of new jobs a necessity in a healthy economy. What is the condition today? From 1952 to 1954, Canada's labour force increased by 122,000. The rate of increase in new jobs tapered off during those years. In 1952 there were 34,300 new jobs created in industry. In 1953 that dropped to 23,000, and it is estimated that in 1954 there will be a further drop to 16,200 or less than half the number of new jobs that were created in 1952.
Some propaganda reports, government and business propaganda, find considerable satisfaction in that, notwithstanding the increased unemployment, there was a slight increase in wages and salaries paid in the year 1954. As I have pointed out already, the increase of output per man hour brought about by our improved technological processes, and possibly better management and better labour-management relations, has rendered it necessary and, as a matter of fact, has made it possible for labour to receive an increasingly larger amount in wages and salaries. The most significant fact is that the rate of increase in average hourly wages dropped off substantially in 1954 as compared with earlier years, as a matter of fact as compared with any year since 1946.
Another danger signal that should demand our attention is the fact that the estimates for capital investment and outlays for repairs during the coming year 1955 remain at about the same level as they were in 1954, or about $7,085 million. If these estimates hold true, 1955 will be the first post-war year in which capital investment has not shown an increase. Capital expenditures in 1954 were 3 per cent higher than those of the previous year, 1953. Personal expenditure in consumer goods and services is estimated by the dominion bureau of statistics to be approximately $15-5 billion. No increase in consumer expenditure is expected for 1955.
If consumer expenditure per capita over the recession year 1954 is to be increased or even maintained, and if there is to be no increase in capital investment by private enterprise, then it becomes evident that if we are to continue to increase our national income, as is necessary, and if we are to provide employment, as is necessary, then the policy which the government laid down for itself in the green book of 1945 must be followed. Government expenditures, either on social welfare work or on capital expenditure projects or both, must be stepped up. We ask the question, where and how can government expenditures be increased? We all realize,

of course, that first of all there are the expenditures for the civil service that must of necessity be limited and that must be determined by the standards of efficiency which the government sets for itself and for its employees. Government expenditures may be briefly summed up as follows: first, all current expenditures for goods and services in connection with government services and operations; second, transfer payments, that is social welfare expenditures; third, capital expenditures for roads, buildings, armaments, etc. As I pointed out, the first is of necessity limited. The second can be expanded; and it can be expanded in the best interests of our national economy and of the welfare of the Canadian people if the government decides to do so. And certainly there is ample opportunity for an increase in the third class of government expenditures.
These transfer payments in the form of family allowances, and the like, influence the rise of employment, as they are converted into consumption expenditures. Increased government expenditures on capital projects raise the levels of new investment. The result: Since national income comprises these two forms of expenditures, the national income is automatically raised by an increase in those expenditures.
Certainly there is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that the government has any intention at this session of introducing measures of a nature such as were outlined in their own green book of 1945, and which were then designed to meet just such a situation as faces the country at the present time.
For example, as to the responsibility for the unemployed employables, let me read a few lines from the green book:
As a part of the general arrangement with the provincial governments, the dominion government now proposes to establish a practicable and comprehensive system of assistance to able-bodied unemployed persons as soon as possible, rather than waiting until the need for it actually arises.
I submit the need has actually arisen today. The government has not made provisions in advance of that need, and the time has now come when it should implement that policy because the need is now with us. Here is another statement:
It is thought necessary not to permit the recurrence of the problems of administration being separated from financial responsibility, and to avoid the makeshift arrangements and controversy with provincial governments which otherwise would be almost certain to recur under the old methods of providing relief even though the number of persons involved were small.
The number of persons involved today s no longer small. They are many, and are

increasing. And municipal councils, mayors and reeves from all over the country have been pleading with the federal government to assume responsibility in some measure for these employable unemployed.
Then, one further quotation from this plan of 1945:
The plan proposes acceptance of dominion responsibility for unemployed employables, and provincial and local responsibility for unemployables . . .
And a further quotation:
Payments for unemployment assistance would be made under authority of an appropriation for this purpose, out of the consolidated revenue fund, and not out of the unemployment insurance fund.
Those were the policies the government presented to us in 1945, policies then designed to cope with a situation such as that facing the country today, a policy upon which the present cabinet has turned its back, and which it has repudiated. I submit this is the session of parliament when the government should review the promises it made to the country in that green book of 1945 and, in the light of present economic conditions, it should bring those policies into effect at this session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REFLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before coming to the substance of my remarks, as one who was congratulated about eight years ago on having moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne I wish to join with my colleagues in congratulating the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address. Listening to their speeches at the opening of the session one was led to realize that the constituents in those two ridings had elected two very distinguished members. In the light of the qualifications stated by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to their public service before entering the House of Commons, and keeping in mind the substance of their speeches, we may rest assured that the electors of those two ridings will see that these two members are re-elected at later dates.
On this occasion I do not intend to discuss what might be called the highlights of the speech from the throne. I congratulate the government upon having mentioned and bringing in at this session certain remedial measures for the development of the economy of this country, and also for having introduced a measure dealing with employment which will be beneficial to the labouring class in Canada.
This afternoon I asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) certain questions in connection with the construction of a public building in Winnipeg. I regret there
50433-20J
The Address-Mr. Viau has been so much delay in starting work on this building, and that there is still delay in creating work for labour in the greater Winnipeg area.
If reports are correct, then I must express my disappointment that not only was the contract given to an eastern firm, but that the goods and supplies are to come from eastern Canada. Surely in the greater Winnipeg area of Manitoba we have responsible contracting firms whose bids or tenders could have been accepted. As yet no decision has been taken with respect to subcontracts covering the bulk of the material to be used in the building, and I hope the contracting firm will see fit to invite tenders from responsible manufacturing firms in Manitoba. We have some very able firms manufacturing not only cement and steel but also electrical devices which will be required in the building.
This afternoon it is my intention to address the house publicly as to what I consider abuse by certain government officials at the level of deputy minister, or its equal, in flouting certain laws of parliament, disregarding members of parliament, and treating parliament with contempt. For the last ten years, mostly during sessions of parliament or, at times, between sessions, either by correspondence or by visits to this capital city requesting certain consideration, as a member of parliament I have felt injured by the treatment received from certain officials at the level of deputy minister, or its equal.
The reason I am determined to make this public this afternoon is that one of these criminal injustices occurred last fall in the province of Manitoba, and I warned the deputy minister concerned that I would make it public. I am going to ask for remedial measures to be taken to correct this situation. Naturally in the 40 minutes allotted to me I will not be able to bring before this house all the injustices that have been perpetrated upon valiant, hard-working civil servants throughout this country. I shall limit my remarks, as I said a while ago, to one injustice which occurred in my own province of Manitoba.
I contend that this situation is the result of not having a fully functioning civil service commission as laid down in the Civil Service Act which was passed years ago by this parliament. The act states that there shall be three commissioners who will hold no other office in the civil service or engage in any other employment. We have the chairman on duty as well as one other commissioner, but during the past four years the third commissioner, who represents French-speaking Canada, has spent more of his time' in foreign lands than in the capital city where
300	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Viau he should be in order to carry out his duties according to the act passed by this parliament.
When the Civil Service Act was passed and this commission created, the number of civil servants was not as large as it is now. The number of civil servants has reached the point where three commissioners cannot have full knowledge of the details concerning the thousands and thousands of civil servants employed by this country. So, according to the act, responsibility has been transferred to the deputy heads of the departments. The result has been the creation of this vicious circle which now exists within the civil service of this nation. It is because of this that we had this injustice which was perpetrated in Manitoba last fall.
The deputy heads connive together when they do not want a certain individual, who may be ready to retire in eight or nine months, to be succeeded by his assistant. Then they make application according to the act. This may be legal, but it satisfies that lust for power which exists in the ordinary human being, and the net result is that the title and qualifications of the position are changed along with a change in the salary. But when the assistant is in a position to assume the office, what happens? He finds that he must take part in a competition because the position has been changed and his qualifications do not entitle him to succeed as the head of that branch within the department.
This is not a far-fetched statement; this condition has existed. If my voice could be heard-and no doubt what I say will be noted by the press in a few days-if the crying injustices done to many civil servants could be recorded and presented to a committee of this house, I am satisfied that following the action of that committee application could be made to the governor in council to remove these deputy heads who have abused their office and imposed injustice upon faithful civil servants throughout the country.
A few years ago a vacancy occurred in Manitoba in the Post Office Department. The vacancy was advertised in the usual manner by the civil service commission, by means of a poster issued in its name by the Post Office Department. The successful candidate was not one who pleased the unelected depository of power in the Post Office Department in the capital city. What happened? A board of appeal was set up, consisting of three members. Two members of the civil service commission refused to accept the application of the protege of this unelected


depository of power in the Post Office Department, and the third member submitted a minority report.
When this news reached the capital city a new board of appeal was created, and the third member of the previous board who had submitted a minority report and who represented the Post Office Department was made the chairman. With what result? The result was that the protege was immediately selected to fill the position of inspector for the Post Office Department, over and above the heads of more qualified civil servants in the Post Office Department in the province of Manitoba.
This situation has existed for quite a while. Last fall I was duly informed that one of the post office inspectors in Manitoba, the only French-speaking inspector in the province, was to retire on March 1, 1955. He was ill last year, and it was said that because of his illness he was requested to tender his resignation as of December 1, 1954. Naturally I was quite concerned over whether the principle of bilingualism was going to be maintained in the province of Manitoba. I came down to the capital city, and I was given the assurance by this unelected depository of power in the Post Office Department not only that the principle of bilingualism would be maintained, but that a competition would be held to select a qualified candidate to replace the retiring post office inspector.
I returned to Winnipeg, or rather I should say to St. Boniface, and was there only a few days when I was informed by a responsible official that I should pay no attention to the assurances given to me by the officials of the Post Office Department in Winnipeg because on December 1 Mr. So-and-So would be appointed as inspector or, as they now call it, area superintendent. I flew at my own expense to the capital city and appealed to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote). I inquired if the information I had received was quite correct. His answer was "Yes. Why?"
It was not that he had discovered himself that it was not possible to hold a competition or to name a bilingual candidate in the province of Manitoba, but that he had been informed by the deputy postmaster general, part of this unelected depository of power, that a regulation of the civil service commission had been discovered which stipulated that when there was not 20 per cent Frenchspeaking or English-speaking there was no need of bilingualism in any area in this nation of ours.
The figures were submitted by the deputy postmaster general who had them all prepared, apparently after a long study. They

could only have been obtained through researches by the bureau of statistics and the Post Office Department while the member for St. Boniface was here in the capital city seeking from responsible officials confirmation of the statement that there would be a competition and the principle of bilingualism would be maintained in Manitoba.
The figure given was 18-54 per cent. I know my own province, and I know we have a larger number than that within the area where this postal inspector was going to work. However, I am not going to dispute the fact that we are short 1 per cent. They insisted on this 1 per cent in the Post Office Department, not because they wanted to respect the Civil Service Act, not because the regulation established by the civil service commission said not less than 20 per cent, but because of a lust for power. They wanted this principle established two years ago, and they railroaded it through in the province of Manitoba despite the civil service commission. The post office department of Manitoba will remain with only 1 per cent of Frenchspeaking employees at the level of administration.
I naturally brought this to the attention of the Postmaster General, and I was told I did not understand the regulations of the act. I was reminded of the words of the deputy postmaster general, that as long as he held office he would never appoint anyone who was mediocre, regardless of the large number of French-speaking Canadians living in the province of Manitoba. I suppose the Postmaster General meant that he would only employ those who had a super education, but for him to call French-speaking Canadians mediocre is not only an insult to them and to myself as a member of parliament, but is treating this house with contempt, for such an attitude is directly contrary to the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
One realizes how absurd his attitude is when we recall that the government spent thousands of dollars to have a firm in Toronto investigate the operations of the Post Office Department, and found that the deputy postmaster general was himself inefficient in carrying out his responsibilities. Despite the findings of that investigation that gentleman still carries on, creating injustices such as the one I have mentioned which result in the morale of the employees of the department being kept at a very low ebb.
Not long ago I brought to his attention a tender which was submitted in Ottawa. If my memory serves me right the tender arrived at four o'clock on October 7, 1954,
The Address-Mr. Viau and it related to a contract for over $1 million in the province of Manitoba. As a matter of fact three tenders left Manitoba at 1.20 a.m. on October 7 and arrived in Ottawa at 9.25 a.m. Two were by special delivery and one was by registered mail, but it took seven and a half hours to deliver these three tenders practically just across the street in Ottawa. One of the special delivery letters arrived at defence production at 2.45 p.m., but the other two did not arrive until 4.11 p.m. It appears that Mr. Johnston could do nothing else but refuse the other two contracts because of the regulation. The net result of that transaction was a loss to the taxpayers of $36,000, because one of the delayed contracts carried the lowest tender. That money was lost to the taxpayers because of the inefficiency of the Post Office Department. So here we have an official of the government flouting laws passed by parliament, insulting a member of parliament, and being inefficient in the handling of his responsibilities.
In my own province of Manitoba an official has been appointed to a position in the post office to which he is not entitled. But before dealing with that I would remind the house that not so long ago the Post Office Department, without consulting members of parliament or provincial and civic officials, established what is called a zoning system in greater Winnipeg. That system will never work. It might work in cities such as Toronto, Montreal, or Winnipeg, but certainly not in the greater Winnipeg area. I opposed the introduction of this system, with the result that it is not now in effect in the constituency of St. Boniface. But as an example of just how ridiculous this can be, I have a letter here addressed to "The Postmaster, Winnipeg, 297 Des Meurons," and in brackets after that comes "St. Boniface, Winnipeg, Manitoba". We spend thousands of dollars to educate our children in geography and the civic structure of this country, and here we have officials of the government flouting our beautiful history by implementing a system which makes no sense whatsoever.
Followihg the Woods-Gordon report of last July, post office officials in Ottawa advertised a promotion competition for area superintendents. That is the new name given to postal inspectors. This competition was confined to the Winnipeg area. At that time a certain A. Vermander and Mr. Walker, both postal inspectors, retired, but no vacancy was created and the name of the post was changed to that of area superintendent. After Mr. Vermander was called upon to retire last fall

The Address-Mr. Viau I was given an assurance by the deputy postmaster general that there would be a competition covering the appointment of a bilingual area superintendent in Manitoba. This assurance was given after I came here at my own expense and was ridiculed by the deputy postmaster general and two of his officials, the executive assistant and the director of administration. But on December 1, 1954, a sign in French and English was posted in every office in Manitoba with the following ultimatum to all civil servants employed by the Post Office Department. It is headed "Appeal Notice" and then comes the following:
The department has approved of the following transfer without advertising a formal competition subject to no appeals being sustained.
This is contrary to the Civil Service Act, which states that if there is a vacancy the deputy head of the department must advise the civil service commission, which will take the necessary measures to formally advertise a competition.
But who was the successful candidate? A short time ago I mentioned a certain protege of the deputy assistant to the Postmaster General, and he in fact was the man who was railroaded into the position over the heads of fully qualified members of the civil service in the province of Manitoba. The man who was appointed area superintendent for Winnipeg without a formal competition was Mr. R. J. Emerson. This was done contrary to the act. It denied the French-speaking population of Manitoba the right of employment, and also denied the rights of highly qualified personnel employed in that area.
All I can do now, Mr. Speaker, is to ask the government of Canada to see that the civil service commission acts in accordance with the regulations of the Civil Service Act. The Postmaster General, his deputy or the civil service commission should be called upon to remove Mr. Emerson from office immediately and to advertise a competition for a bilingual area superintendent for Winnipeg. The competition should then be carried out in accordance with the act. We have the qualified personnel, and it is high time some of the ministers of this government inquired closely into the actions of some of their deputies, particularly when it comes to an appointment of the kind I have mentioned. Action should be taken when an injustice has been done and when a member of parliament brings that privately to the minister's attention, for it will then be possible to handle the matter without the necessity of a member of parliament having to make the matter public as I have now done.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REFLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first wish to add my word of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They are both young members. Not only did they speak well but their material was well prepared.
In so far as the speech from the throne is concerned, I was disappointed that mention was not made of matters which I consider to be of urgent importance. I was glad to see that some measure was to be introduced to deal with war veterans allowances. I feel that such a measure is overdue. I can never agree with the statement made by one hon. member to the effect that he did not believe men had aged prematurely ten years in the war. I think it is a well-established fact that the men of the first war particularly aged prematurely at least ten years in their period of service. There is no special yardstick by which the effect can be diagnosed, but many of these veterans with excellent service are in need of higher payments owing to the present cost of living and the cost of maintaining their homes.
This debate on the address is of value to this house because it gives members an opportunity to present to parliament conditions in their own ridings, and as well to call the attention of parliament to the position of the country as a whole. I cannot be accused in any way of talking blue ruin in this country because I do not believe this to be a fact, for the future of Canada is possibly brighter than that of any other country on the globe. Canada covers 3,695,000 square miles and has 13,000 miles of coast line on the great lakes and the seas. The territory of Canada is about the same size as that of Europe and larger than that of the United States. There are 300 million acres of arable land in Canada, and of that 300 million acres only about half are cultivated. The surface has only been scratched of our vast mineral resources. Industry has grown, and in 73 years the value of manufactured goods has made progress from a few million to more than $5 billion.
It is true that there are matters of urgent importance affecting this country. We find marked unemployment, falling markets and an unfortunate economic balance in agriculture where the price received by the farmers for their commodities is going down and the farmer finds himself faced with the present high cost of consumer goods which he finds it necessary to buy.
Much credit has been taken by this government in past years and even up to the present time with regard to the growth and

the prosperity of Canada. My faith in Canada is so great that, in spite of adverse conditions, I believe Canada will still grow and will still prosper. I am reminded of the statement made years ago by that delightful figure in the world of entertainment, Will Rogers. He was not only an entertainer but also a philosopher. Once, when discussing the political situation in the United States- that of Democrats versus Republicans-he made a statement that I think could be well taken to heart by those who argue blue ruin. He said, "This country is too big to be destroyed by any political party".
I wish to present to you today the position of the agriculturalists and more particularly that of the dairy farmers, not only in my own riding but in the whole of the dominion. I find that there is considerable misunderstanding with regard to the difficulties faced by this great industry, especially on the part of those who are not actively engaged in the industry itself. The county of Lanark has been recognized for years as an important centre in the dairy industry, and over the years it has been especially noted for its production of Cheddar cheese manufactured both for export and for domestic consumption.
It should be appreciated that dairy farming is an occupation which requires many hours of hard work. It is not merely a matter of a six-day week. Even on Sundays cows must be milked and cared for, and milk must be prepared and cooled in order that it may reach market on Monday in good condition. Not only is there this consideration, but in order to build up a good dairy herd and secure high production, there must be constant care and supervision. Any dairy farmer can tell you that it is an expensive proposition for him during the years when he builds up a good dairy herd. There is also the cost of maintaining equipment such as silos and barns. Of late years the cost of labour has been so high that it is a factor which must be taken into account in the cost of production.
As an industry, dairying is one of the most important in Canada. It is not generally realized that 450,000 farmers depend upon the dairy industry as their source of income. Indirectly two million Canadians derive part or all of their income from this source. That includes those engaged in production, distribution, processing and supplying various services and equipment. It contributes more than $600 million to our national commerce. Food, of course, is the main product, and this includes butter, cheese, cream, bottled milk, powdered milk and many other types of food provided by dairy herds. I mention these facts in order to bring before this house and the public the importance of this industry.
The Address-Mr. Blair
Last November the bureau of statistics showed a drop in the cost of living index, and it was to be noted that the lower figure was accounted for by food prices. This figure would have been considerably lower were it not for the fact that the cost of other commodities showed a rise or remained at their former figures. In plain language, the drop in the cost of living was due to the farmer. Reports at the end of the year showed that the drop in farm income in 1954 amounted to 13 per cent. To one section of our population this was a pleasant thing, because cheaper farm commodities meant cheaper food. But there is something more serious which has been generally disregarded by a large portion of the public, namely the drop in farm income; and the drop in general food prices has had much to do with the jobs of ordinary Canadians.
We are hearing all sorts of reasons, even in this house, as the causes of unemployment. It has been called seasonal, and even the weather has been blamed. But everybody who talks about it apparently avoids the obvious explanation. One reason is plainly outstanding. Far too many farmers have not available the cash with which to buy manufactured goods, nor have they the cash when it is necessary to employ labour themselves. We must remember that the 450,000 dairy farmers, together with their families and all the people who are connected with the dairy trade, consume large quantities of manufactured goods. We cannot afford to have the income of that large group of people so reduced that their buying power will be impaired.
The buying power of the farmers is required in connection with goods manufactured by Canadian industry, by Canadian labour. When the buying power of the farmers becomes impaired-and let us remember that there are several hundred thousand farmers-there is a slow-down of our industrial economy, and we have the kind of unemployment that we are experiencing in Canadian business today.
Under present conditions in Canada it is an excellent thing to be able to obtain cheap food. I repeat that the drop in our consumer price index, or the cost of living record, is mainly due to the fact that there has been a drop in the price of food. In this connection it is well to remember that cheaper food is related to jobs; I refer to jobs of people employed in industry and manufacture. There is little good in the saving of a few cents on the cost of a spread for bread, or a pound of processed cheese, if the result is going to be that more Canadians are thrown out of jobs. Let me again emphasize the fact that in this case food costs are related to jobs.
304	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blair
The average farm family buys about four times as much goods of every description as does the average urban family. The farmer buys not only the necessities for his household but, in addition, buys largely the products of industry in the nature of farm implements and various types of goods or machinery which he uses in his work on the farm. When the farmer makes less money he does not buy, and the people who are employed in other industries, who live and are consumers in urban centres, should remember that when they demand cheaper food they are, without thinking, contributing to unemployment within their own country. I do not blame people for wishing to buy their food more cheaply. This is only natural with the present high cost of living, but one must take a broad and long-term view of the matter.
I now come to the question of the importation of New Zealand cheese. There is an old saw about carrying coals to Newcastle, and this is about the most surprising deal one could imagine. In Canada we have cheese to give away and now more of it is being hauled thousands of miles across the Pacific, adding to the confusion. There has been some mystery about this deal, because it is extremely difficult under the circumstances to find why such a deal was ever made. Under the deal 2,250,000 pounds of New Zealand cheese are being imported into Canada at a time when about 10 million pounds more cheese is reported in Canada than there was a year ago. If an importer can bring in New Zealand cheese, this takes the props from under any Canadian dairy product.
Further, if what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) says means unrestricted imports of cheese and powdered and processed milk, then within six months Canadian products will be at the world price, which is approximately $2 a hundred for milk. It may be argued that this New Zealand cheese is only one shipment, is not likely to be repeated, and is not a matter of great moment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated in the house a few days ago that no further imports of New Zealand cheese are expected for six or nine months.
Apparently a verbal agreement was made in 1952 whereby New Zealand agreed not to send cheese to Canada for the reason that Canadian producers were having difficulty in selling to the British market. The Ontario cheese producers' association has been working, at considerable expense to the organization, to stabilize this department of the dairy industry of the country. In fact it has raised over a million dollars for the purpose of exporting Canada's surplus. Now the cheese



The Address-Mr. Blair
The truth is that not only farmers but other Canadian producers find themselves being priced out of world markets. If all other things were equal farmers would be glad to cut their prices so they could export, provided they would not be expected to do all the cutting. Farmers and manufacturers in other countries can sell for less in the world markets because their costs are less, wages are lower and the standard of living is lower. Canadian farmers have made a substantial contribution, but this has been offset by high processing and handling charges. Canadian consumers are not receiving the full benefits of lower farm prices, because costs over which the farmer has no control have risen.
Turning to another subject, I may say that I was interested in a speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) in Montreal in November. He indicated in that speech that he found taxes in Canada pretty high- those were his words-and he was amazed that Canadian citizens put up with them. I enjoyed hearing someone in the government say this, especially the Minister of Finance. Evidently the minister is aware of the burden on industry and the people in general.
There is no doubt about the requirements for defence and general maintenance, and allowance must be made for increased services. But if our industries are going to succeed in a competitive market there must be a cutting down of costs. This must start with a real program of economy within the government. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that it is true of human nature that where a person has been living high, with almost unlimited money to spend, it is sometimes difficult to learn how to restrict unnecessary spending. I suggest that in this connection study should be given to the report of the Auditor General.
There has been a great deal of discussion on the matter of cutting costs in order that we may export, and a tendency to blame various groups or sections of our people. It is sometimes difficult for any one group to make the first move because of the cost of living. Hardship is always involved if the balance between income and the cost of living is disturbed. The workers in any industry wage a continuous struggle to maintain the balance between wages and the cost of living.
Our great neighbour to the south, the United States, is almost self-contained. They have a domestic market of 160 million people. There is complete interchangeability of goods among the 48 states. Again I cannot help but point out that our domestic market is only 15 million people. This brings up the question of the importance of immigration, and


the building up of our population as a longterm plan cannot be overemphasized. If we doubled our population that would give us a domestic market which would absorb more and more of our industrial products, including agricultural products. The development of our natural resources would mean many more workers, more buyers of domestic consumer goods and a greatly increased domestic market. It therefore follows that in such a long-term program of development there would be more employment for Canadian workers.
Certain factors must be taken into consideration in meeting competition. Taxes add to the cost of production and place our industries at an unfair disadvantage. When industry suffers in this way, unemployment is created. Industrial growth is hampered by high corporation taxes. Increased consumer buying power stimulates industrial expansion, and in turn creates more jobs. Steps taken toward lowering taxes would decrease production costs and help our industries to meet competition, not only in the domestic field but in the export markets as well.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that there is no mention of economy in the speech from the throne. Every year the government says the Canadian taxpayer must produce more money. Taxes can defeat their own ends. If the tax levy is at too high a rate, production and expansion in industry are decreased and in the end the tax will produce less revenue than a somewhat lower rate. A corporation tax of 49 per cent would leave little room for industrial expansion, cutting of costs, and hence ability to meet foreign competition.
I am fully aware of the difficulties involved in world trading today, but again I point out that under present conditions we cannot afford to sacrifice the great Canadian dairy industry. The international tension that exists today makes it necessary, for our own preservation, that we maintain this important industry as part of our program of preparedness.
The farm implement industry now has marked unemployment. In this connection I wish to briefly discuss the Colombo plan. Canada has voted $100 million to help the economic development of south and southeast Asia, and to help raise the standard of living of the 570 million people in that area. The Department of External Affairs, in discussing the Colombo plan, has stated:
India's food problem is tremendous.
There is never enough food produced in India to feed the population at even the minimum standard to which they are accustomed.

The shortage of food amounts to five million tons. According to the same statement the government of India seems to be fully aware of the desperate need to close this gap, and its five-year development plan concentrates on increased agricultural production. We are told that India devotes 17-5 per cent of investment capital to the improvement and extension of agriculture, and 21 per cent to irrigation. It would seem that it is India's policy to grow more food for her people.
Apparently it is left to the country receiving the help under the Colombo plan to decide how the money should be expended. If the policy of India is to grow more food it will mean bringing more land under cultivation and improving the farming methods on the new land as well as the areas already under crop. The improvement could be carried out in some ways by using certain types of Canadian farm machinery.
Of the $51 million Canada sent to aid India, we find that none of the money has been spent on farm machinery. Pakistan and Ceylon received the remaining $48 million, and of that sum only $200,000 has been spent on farm machinery. Canada sent to India locomotives, electrical equipment, boilers and the like, but no plows, tractors or other farm implements. It would seem that in India, which is concentrating on increasing the production of foodstuffs and has reclaimed two million acres of land, added to another eight million acres which were brought under irrigation, it is poor policy to continue working on land by primitive methods which in years gone by have never yielded adequate crops.
I am aware of the difficulty in teaching these new methods as opposed to the ancient methods in some of those countries; but if sufficient food is to be grown then new methods will have to be adopted. In view of the fact that the farm implement industry in Canada is going through a difficult period from lack of orders, I suggest that measures be taken to increase the shipment of those commodities to such countries as India which are receiving help under the Colombo plan. Certainly $200,000 worth of implements is a very small proportion of the $100 million Canada has already expended. I believe expenditures under the Colombo plan represent money well spent, and will bring excellent results. But as I have suggested, it would help the farm implement industry in Canada if a due proportion of Canada's expenditures were to consist of agricultural implements.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always very favourably impressed by the high level of debate and the
The Address-Mr. Enfield effective presentations one hears in the house, to the point where sometimes I am a little diffident about making my own contribution. I wish particularly, however, to congratulate the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply. The hon. member for Verdun made a most eloquent presentation. This is understandable in one who comes from a province where fine speakers and great orators are the order of the day. And most certainly one must take justifiable pride in the clear, concise and comprehensive remarks of one's closer associate from the Toronto area, the hon. member for Trinity.
It is understandable that many hon. members are most concerned about the unemployment situation. I think we all feel that, so long as one person who wants work is unable to find it, for him the distress is great indeed. During the past two years we have seen a change in economic conditions on a worldwide scale. Competition has increased greatly in the selling field in all parts of the world, particularly with the economic come-back of the European countries, including Germany and Great Britain. We have witnessed a change from a wartime economy, with defence expenditures predominant, to a peacetime economy and certainly to a more normal period of economic growth and change. This change has been followed with some anxiety and certainly with a great deal of interest by the investor, the businessman and the worker.
Fortunately there has been no great economic upheaval, although there has been some economic upset. We see a residue of unemployment now resulting in Canada. The latest figures I have from the dominion bureau of statistics indicate that on November 30 of last year 214,000 persons were out of work and seeking employment. This was the total in a labour force of 5,417,000 workers, or a little more than 3h per cent of the total labour force.
Without wishing to minimize the seriousness of unemployment generally I should like to draw a comparison between the monthly unemployment figures of the years 1953 and 1954, to show the increase per month during that time. For example, in March 1953 there were 172,000 persons seeking employment and in the corresponding month of 1954 there were 318,000, or an increase of 146,000. In April of 1953 we find the figure to be 165,000 and in 1954 to be 303,000, or a slightly smaller increase of 138,000. For May of 1953 the figure was 114,000, and in 1954 it was 217,000, or an increase of 103,000. In June, July and August the increase per month was 95,000,
82,000	and 83,000, respectively. The same proportions applied for September, but in

The Address-Mr. Enfield October the increase had dropped to 68,000 and in November the increase over the corresponding month in the previous year had dropped to 63,000.
I know the argument will be offered that one can do anything with figures, but I do suggest that they indicate a strong trend. The problem is serious, but it was not as serious at the end of that period, namely in November of 1954, as it was in March of that year. And I think we have good reason to hope that this trend will continue. I do not share the view of the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) who felt that unemployment would continue to increase to a point where we would have about 600,000 unemployed before the close of the winter months. If the trend I have indicated continues I feel the situation at that time will be somewhat less serious than it was last winter.
In Toronto we are very fortunate in this respect. In a recent issue of the Globe and Mail there is a comment by an official of the unemployment insurance commission to the effect that there is the equivalent of a little more than one person unemployed for every 28 employed in that city. We know that unemployment figures vary from municipality to municipality and from area to area, and that the unemployment situation is most serious in some areas. I do feel that in those places the intelligent allocation of public works and projects is most important to alleviate local situations.
While I am on this subject I will point out that an awkward problem does exist in connection with the relief of the employable unemployed. I know the federal government has been charged with complete responsibility for these persons. The statement is made that in the green book, which is the record of the dominion-provincial conference of 1945 and 1946, the dominion government made certain proposals in this connection. I would point out, however, that when an offer is made it does not constitute a binding contract until such offer has been accepted. At that time, as we know, the two largest and richest provinces did not accept the offer. Ontario entered into a separate tax agreement in 1948, and Quebec has not as yet entered into any agreement. Therefore the legal responsibility still rests, of course, with the provinces for the relief of the employable unemployed.
It is true that we have taken on the task of providing an unemployment insurance act. Many people feel that because we have done so we should assume complete responsibility for unemployment. From a practical point of view it might be better to administer

this type of thing by one government and with one administration. Perhaps that is the only really businesslike way in which the matter can be handled. But you cannot take on a financial responsibility which by virtue of the constitution rests upon the provinces unless you enter into some agreement with them to safeguard yourself at the time you take over. When a dominion-provincial conference is held in the future I feel that this question should be placed high on the agenda, and it should be decided definitely where the responsibility will lie.
When we look at the third quarter of 1954 and the beginning of 1955 we see a feeling of buoyancy and optimism expressed by our business leaders, by our newspaper columnists and commentators. Despite the unemployment I feel I have caught some of that feeling of buoyancy and optimism. I think as a federal government we should do all we can to foster an optimistic outlook.
One of the strongest pillars of employment, in metropolitan Toronto in any event, has been our housing program. The government must feel most gratified indeed at the unqualified success of the National Housing Act over the past year. We know that on the national level in 1953 some $280 million was invested in National Housing Act loans. For the first nine months of 1954 that figure had increased to $418 million, nearly twice as much for just the first nine months of that year. It showed a tremendous increase.
In the Toronto area some 7,500 homes were built under National Housing Act auspices in 1953. In the first nine months of 1954 that figure had doubled, to 15,000. The manager of the local office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Scarborough tells me that over 60 per cent of all National Housing Act homes built in metropolitan Toronto were constructed in that township. I am quite proud of that. Over 7,000 homes were constructed during the year in Scarborough, which is certainly most gratifying.
The building of homes has a tremendous impact upon our economy in the way of providing employment and an outlet for investment. In this connection I should like to quote from a speech delivered by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) to the Electrical club in Montreal on December 1 last. The minister said:	.
By the end of the year Canadians will have spent about $1,250,000,000 on new housing during 1954 alone. This is 5 per cent of our gross national product. This program means expenditures on materials of over $680 million, and employment for a labour force of an average of about 100,000 men for a full year on site alone.
We are all anxious to keep the housing program or housing boom-I think I can use

that word-continuing at its present level, if not increasing. We must look at some of the problems involved in this situation. If we are to bring housing into a more effective field of demand where it will be progressively necessary to build more houses, then the price of housing must be brought within the reach of the average income groups.
One of the largest items of cost in connection with housing, at least in the metropolitan Toronto area, is the cost of serviced land. Municipalities hesitate to impose increasingly heavy tax burdens on the taxpayers in these communities. The largest single item of cost to the community is that of providing schools. I noticed in the January 7 issue of the Toronto Daily Star that the township of North York, a great part of which is in my riding, has a program for schools that will cost more than that of any municipality in the country. The cost of education falls directly upon the home owners. In my riding this accounts for 50 per cent, or in some cases 60 per cent, of the real estate tax bill. This is really a crippling proportion. As I say, municipal councils hesitate to embark upon new housing projects if this taxation has to be increased.
We are often requested as a federal government to contribute toward the cost of education. Under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act, which allocate powers to the provinces and the dominion, we do not have jurisdiction to interfere with or to make direct contributions toward elementary schooling, or toward secondary schooling for that matter. We have made contributions to the universities which have been accepted and administered by the provinces. I think in a future dominion-provincial conference the question of federal contributions toward education might be usefully dealt with.
We could confer a direct benefit upon municipalities by allowing real estate taxes to be deducted from net taxable income for income tax purposes. I realize that this is not the first time this has been suggested in the house. On checking Hansard I notice that the former member for York West, the late Rodney Adamson, at one time made this very suggestion. There may be more equitable ways to reduce taxes if that is what we have in mind. I feel that this would not be so much a reduction in taxes as an adjustment to encourage the continued expansion of the housing industry. I think perhaps it is worthy of some consideration. I admit that I have not attacked all sides or looked at all the considerations that might arise in
The Address-Mr. Enfield connection with his suggestion, and I must admit that the suggestion may be considered a selfish one on my part because more than 95 per cent of my constituents are home owners.

No, I do not have any estimate of the cost of this reduction to the federal treasury.
The question arises as to the application of the sales tax and excise tax in connection with supplies purchased by school boards for maintenance and construction. We saw this principle invoked last year in the reduction of excise taxes on certain equipment purchased by municipalities. It might be well worth looking at the school situation from this point of view.
Tax reductions do not always mean reductions in the actual revenue collected and perhaps that was what was in the mind of the hon. gentleman who asked the question a moment ago. This may seem paradoxical, but we all know that often some reduction in taxes will produce an increase in economic activity, the fruits of which are greater revenue or perhaps the same revenue as before.
I do not like to think of taxes being decreased because that raises connotations in the minds of businessmen that the government is on an economic drive. I would not like to see government expenditure decrease because I think that would be a very bad thing for the economy at this time.
Since 1946 we have seen a tremendous expansion in business and in the economic field throughout the country. We have an expanding economy, and while it is expanding we enjoy more or less full employment. It is necessary that we sell the fruits of our labour abroad. We have to trade to survive, and I would like to commend the government on taking a stand for the ideal of free trade. The liberal trading policies of Canada -and I use the small letter "1" there-have been questioned lately as never before, and that is perhaps natural. Canada's trading pattern before the war was well established. We applied the sterling balances in our trade with Britain to the deficit in our trade with the United States, and thereby maintained a balance of trade between the two areas.
After the second world war sterling area restrictions were strengthened; there were increases on quotas-quotas that still exist- and, of course, the pound was unconvertible. The pattern of trade under these circumstances changed. Britain and other sterling area countries were unable to take the

The Address-Mr. Enfield volume of commodities they previously took because they did not have the dollars with which to pay for them, and more and more the emphasis was placed on our trade with the United States. That was a natural and in my opinion inevitable result.
We could have joined the sterling area, but I do not think anyone would seriously suggest this proposition. It ignores the economic realities of our situation, which include the close geographical proximity of the United States. It would also ignore the North American outlook which is part and parcel of Canada and the United States. Our equipment and organization in Canada is North American in its scope and details. We have great and numerous inter-company relationships between the two countries which is an altogether desirable and inevitable consequence of our geographical proximity. There is a terrific pressure for United States capital to seek an investment outlet under profitable private enterprise. The United States is our chief source of foreign capital, and it will be more so.
We recall the Paley commission, which was set up in the United States to study their sources of natural energy, hydro, coal, oil, and uranium. The commission, I believe, reported in 1952 to the United States congress that their home sources of energy were on the decline and had passed their peak. Every day means the consumption of more energy in industry and in homes in the United States. Canada, on the other hand, has tremendous sources of energy that have yet to be developed, and some that have yet to be discovered, while the United States will be forced to look more and more outside their own country for sources of cheap natural energy.
Developments in British Columbia in the field of hydroelectric power are indicative of the trend. We see ourselves exporting tremendous quantities of hydroelectric power in the form of aluminum from British Columbia and some other parts of the country. What then is the result of this trend? Two-thirds of our import and export trade at the present time is with the United States. Roughly, we take about 26 per cent of all United States exports. We are their best and largest single customer. We take more goods from the United States than all the Latin-American countries combined, and indeed more than all the European countries combined.
We still have surpluses, of course, particularly in our farm products. It has been suggested that in order to promote convertibility of the pound we should loan money to Britain. This is a good suggestion, but it


ignores the fact that British traders of late have been given more or less a free hand in the purchase of lumber, wheat, and metals, and they do not want to borrow money to purchase items which are not essential to their economy. It is all very well to suggest that we loan Britain the money with which they can purchase our goods and thereby assist them in their drive toward convertibility. It takes two to make a bargain, and it is very doubtful if Britain is disposed to borrow money. Her aim is to get out of debt and strengthen her economy, which in itself will provide the answer to convertibility. That answer lies in free trade.
The general agreement on tariffs and trade embodies the old empire preferences, because they are acceptable to the countries taking part in the agreement. Under the circumstances we have seen an increasing amount of multilateral trade between sterling and dollar countries, and the situation is improving continuously. However, convertibility is not something you just pick out of the air. It will take time and patience on the part of the countries involved to reach that point when we will have the benefit of trade with the sterling area free of quotas and restrictions.
In the meantime, our government is pressing for the provisions of the general agreement on tariffs and trade, and urging that they be fully carried out. I think the recent journey of our ministers of trade and commerce (Mr. Howe), finance (Mr. Harris) and external affairs (Mr. Pearson) to Washington was an imaginative, courageous and highly commendable action; and although it may be some time before we see any change on the part of the government of the United States we can certainly say that we have tried to impress upon the United States the importance and urgency of carrying out the provisions of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. From that point of view I think the negotiations were highly successful.
We have seen a great economic and spiritual conflict in foreign relations among the different countries of the world. We hope that out of that conflict, as is very often the case, a firmer understanding towards peaceful development will emerge. Despite our problems the Canadian nation has been pulling its weight as a world power. When we have been called upon to do so we have contributed to the defence of the free nations. We took our part in the Korean conflict. We participated fully in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I think the free world is better for the 12 squadrons of fighters we now have operating in Germany. We have an

important role in Indo-China. We did our part in the Korean negotiations. I feel that our spokesmen are admired and respected at the United Nations.
On the economic front, the Canadian dollar is still the world's strongest currency. We shall obviously have our bad moments, but underneath it all there is an underlying economic, spiritual and philosophic strength which none of us yet fully appreciates. I feel that we should have no fear for the future.
