speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank you indeed for your courtesy at five minutes to six in asking for unanimous consent to call it six o'clock. It helped me to avoid starting my speech only to break into it for the dinner recess.
In the debate on the speech from the throne I wish to speak on behalf of the people of the constituency of Macleod, which I have had the honour to represent for some years.
The constituency of Macleod is quite diversified in several ways. There are the Turner valley oil fields at the northern and western corner, and while they are not quite as active today as they were some years ago, nevertheless there is quite a little industry in that part of the constituency. Then there is the great foothills country on the east slope of the Rocky mountains, which is a tremendous ranching region. Toward the south and west is the coal mining area of the Crowsnest pass. We have a sugar beet industry in the southern and eastern corner, and most of the central region is composed of a rich and vast wheat growing area.
In the time allotted to me in this debate I do not expect to be able to speak on all the various things that affect my constituency. There will be time for that later during the session, when I will be able to speak on behalf of every part of this diversified riding. But I do wish to pay some attention at the present time to a situation that I think is most serious. I refer to the cash position of the farmers of the west. I refer to those of
The Address-Mr. Hansell my constituency in particular, because I represent them; but I am sure many others who represent farming regions of western Canada will agree with me that this matter is of grave importance. During the summer I attended and spoke at a number of meetings called by various farm organizations, as well as having the opportunity, of course, of talking to many farmers privately. I found that to many of them the situation was serious to the extent that they did not have enough money to get along.
I think we all realize that over the past number of years the farmers have not complained too much. Prices have been fair to good, and for the most part crop conditions have been reasonably good. There have been some areas where we have had crop failures, and of course the situation in Saskatchewan this year is very bad. But the fact that there is a surplus of grain does not help the farmer if he has no money at the moment. In my investigation I found this meant that certain farmers were in danger of having foreclosures made on the things they had bought. Machine companies were beginning to tighten up, and other companies that had financed purchases of the farmers were beginning to take steps if payments were not made right on time.
Some farmers came to me and said they had difficulty in meeting their current expenses to the extent of having to ask the grocer and others to wait for a little while. It is a well known fact that oil and gas companies came to a point in their operations where they instituted a cash on delivery policy. While we are very thankful in our part of the country, Mr. Speaker, for a measure of prosperity over the years, it must not be thought that all our farmers are wealthy. Some of them have not done too badly, but there are others who by no stretch of the imagination can be considered to be wealthy or in a favourable financial position.
Young men who have started to farm are finding it particularly difficult to get along when they have no cash. The same is true of some young veterans who have started afresh. They do not complain about the treatment they have received from the Department of Veterans Affairs or the policy that has been laid down for them by the government, but they are having difficulty now in financing their way because they do not have cash.
Then again there are the small farmers. In my part of the country it is pretty difficult to be successful with a small farm at any time. Wheat growing is pretty general among the farmers of that particular area, and it is considered that a farmer there finds it pretty tough unless he has a fairly large amount of

The Address-Mr. Hansell land. The small farmer finds it hard to get along today, particularly in view of the fact that he cannot sell his wheat and consequently does not have any cash.
It might be said that there is a surplus of grain, and most of these farmers have wheat in their bins. That may be so. Perhaps there was a day when the saying was true that "wheat in the bin was as good as money in the bank", but that cannot be said today. It is not true today because while they may have a surplus of grain stored on their farms, they cannot meet their bills if they have no cash. Foreclosures of one kind and another are threatened, and that is not a very healthy or happy situation.
I think we will all agree that the government has given no consideration whatsoever to alleviating this serious condition. I believe they should have done so, because there are ways of alleviating what may be more or less a temporary condition. However, if the temporary condition lasts too long it is then more than temporary; it becomes a condition that one must expect from one crop year to another, and that is not good.
I claim that the government could have taken steps to devise some plan whereby farmers with wheat in storage on their farms could have received some money, at least enough to get by on. I see no reason why the government could not have guaranteed the banks against loss in case they lent money on the farmers' wheat. They could have done that as a sort of bridge-the-gap policy. The government guarantees bank loans today in many other respects. We have the Canadian farm loan board, the loans of which are guaranteed by the government. We have the national housing scheme under which the government guarantees the loans of those people who borrow money for housing. The banks are now engaged in these lending operations, so it is not a new thing for the government to guarantee the banks and lending institutions against loss. It does seem to me that the government could have taken some steps along that line to help the farmers.
There is another suggestion. In my opinion it would not have been difficult for the wheat board itself to advance payments on the grain the farmers have in their granaries. It would be tantamount to taking the grain ahead of time. After all, the wheat ultimately has to go through the wheat board for sale, and I see no reason why the wheat board could not have adopted some plan of that kind under the direction of a government policy.
This would have been of tremendous help to the farmers who were in need. It would not be necessary for the farmers to take

advantage of these loans if they did not need them, but the farmers who find they cannot pay their grocery bills, cannot meet operating expenses on their farms, cannot pay for oil and gas deliveries, cannot pay for truck repairs and a lot of other things, could have taken advantage of loans if they had been made available. I do believe the government could have done something along those lines.
Now, what of the future? It is wintertime now, but the first thing you know spring will be here. The farmers will have to put in their crops. Again perhaps the oil companies and other companies dealing with farmers will go on a cash delivery basis. What is going to happen? Are the farmers to continue in this predicament? I urge the government, in the strongest possible terms, to give serious consideration to this most grievous problem, and during this session to introduce appropriate legislation to deal with this matter. I am sure western farmers would be pleased if something of that kind could be accomplished. Nobody would be out of pocket, and the farmers would be pleased with that action by this government. I ask that the government take appropriate measures along these lines as soon as possible.
During this session I shall deal with other matters affecting my constituency at such times and on such appropriate occasions as will afford more effective discussion. I turn now to another matter upon which I think there is need for some comment. We have heard a good deal in this debate, particularly from our C.C.F. friends, about what they regard as the evil of our private enterprise system. Frankly, of course, we in this corner of the house, we Social Crediters throughout Canada, support an effective private enterprise system. We recognize that in the past there have been certain abuses of the system by certain individuals or corporations. However, that is no reason for blaming the system as a whole. We believe that these abuses could be eliminated and that the private enterprise system could function effectively and efficiently for the good of all the citizens of Canada, providing them with incomes and at the same time giving them the freedom that free enterprise should give.
We believe private enterprise could become extremely effective under a proper financial policy. It does seem to be a sort of stock in trade argument for our C.C.F. friends, whom we have learned to like as men, to blame private enterprise for everything. It is significant that they never say, at least I have never heard any of them on any occasion, how they would handle any problem for which they blame private enterprise.

If an economic problem exists they never appraise it in the light of all its factors; they never seek for a proper solution. They just blame private enterprise and rap the knuckles of this Liberal government or any government throughout the country for what they claim is that government's loyalty to the private enterprise system.
While I say that, after a good many years of observation and study, and a good many years during which I have been responsible for appraising political trends, I have come to the conclusion that in reality there is no more dangerous socialist party than the present Liberal party in Canada. Now, that may sound strange to some ears.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to extend my sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Perhaps I should say a word about the very entertaining speech by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) to which we have just listened. I tried to follow him when he endeavoured to prove that the Liberals were really socialists in disguise. Of course, it would be difficult to prove that to me. However, I was interested in his reasoning. He said that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had outlined various C.C.F. proposals, and suggested that the Liberals had put those proposals into effect. I do not recall exactly what proposals the C.C.F. suggested, but the hon. member for Macleod said they must have been socialist proposals because they were suggested by the C.C.F. I tried to remember the items listed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which the Liberals put through and I recalled unemployment insurance, old age pensions, blind pensions, and, I believe, family allowances. In this regard, however, I would remind the hon. member that the Social Credit party also supported those measures, and I suppose on the same reasoning they are therefore socialist.
That is the full extent to which I shall try to answer the hon. member for Macleod, because I confess I was not very successful


in following his reasoning. I closely followed speeches by members of the official opposition and attempted to detect what faults they had to find in the past administration of this country, and what they had to suggest by way of remedy. It seems to me they concentrated on two things; first, the question of rising unemployment, and second the reduction in export trade. I shall deal with some of their suggestions during the course of my remarks, but first of all I wish to deal with some of the positive achievements of the present government which, I believe, fully warrant the support they have received over the past 19 years.
I believe the most important consideration for all of us is the extent to which we have contributed as a nation, under the leadership of the present government, to the preservation of peace. The London-Paris agreement will shortly be laid before the house. That agreement is designed to promote the solidarity of the western world against the only possible aggressor, imperialist communism. With regard to this agreement, in my opinion there can be no doubt as to what we should do in the light of history.
We were often told in the past that if it had been made plain to German leaders before the outbreak of the 1914 war that they were going to find Great Britain arrayed against them, they would never have plunged the nations of the world into war. Certainly I believe it is fair to assume that had they known they would ultimately find ranged against them not only Great Britain but the United States as well, the 1914 war would never have taken place.
Coming now to the outbreak of the war in 1939, it was thought at that time that if Great Britain made it plain that if Hitler committed further acts of aggression against Poland there was no doubt where Great Britain would stand, it was hoped that would deter Hitler. Apparently Hitler was not convinced that Great Britain meant business. Also I think it is again fair to say that if Hitler had been sure that not only would Great Britain enter the war with the determination which she ultimately displayed, but that he would find the great power of the United States also ranged against him, he would never have started the war in 1939.
Surely we should learn from these events. If we who are opposed to aggression make it quite plain to the aggressor that we mean business and will stick together and fight against anyone who endangers the peace of the world, then it seems to me that in all probability war can be prevented. Therefore in our attempt to unify the western world we should thereby make it plain to the only

potential aggressor in the world today that if she starts a war she will find the entire western world unified against her. I believe that by taking this step we will be going as far as we possibly can in this field to ensure the peace of the world.
It seems to me that when communist groups in all parts of the world try to undermine the will and determination of the free world to unite in strength and common purpose and make their enmity plain, then it is quite clear where their interests lie. People who believe in freedom, democracy, and peace surely should not follow the lead of communist stooges, witting or unwitting, in this or any other country.
There is another feature of the international situation in which our government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), have played a very worthy part, and that is in their support of the efforts of the United Nations to help the economically undeveloped nations, particularly in the Far East. I do not believe there is any doubt that rather than starve to death people will fight and it should not be overlooked that force will not indefinitely maintain world peace if it is not established on justice and fair play between one section of mankind and another.
I therefore strongly support the policy of the United Nations designed to assist economically undeveloped nations so they can increase their own productive capacity, for I am convinced that such schemes will assist in the preservation of world peace. Canada, by her support of such United Nations schemes, and also the Colombo plan, is assisting materially toward that end, and I believe Canada has played a very worthy part in all these programs.
A proper attitude toward the less fortunate people of the world is a very important feature of the struggle for peace. They are fellow human beings. We do not want them to swamp us by coming into this country in too great numbers, but we certainly must help them to increase their production and allow their exports into this country in sufficient quantities to buy enough food so their people shall not starve to death.
It is a question of whether we would rather trade than fight. On the ground of simple Christian fair play, or on the ground of self-interest, it seems to me that we should be prepared to reduce the barriers to trade, and permit those people to obtain the wherewithal to feed their teeming populations. It seems to me that Canada's work along that
The Address-Mr. Tucker line has been extremely worthy. She has taken the lead in promoting the elimination of the barriers to trade.
I might say it appeared to me that one of the bases of the opposition criticism was that the government had gone too far in that respect, and that we should be processing more of our raw materials at home. That was the basis upon which Sir John A. Macdonald got his nationalist policy accepted, namely that we should cease to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the United States. The only way we could process more of our raw materials in this country is in some way by quotas or tariffs to protect the industries which might process those raw materials. If we begin to put on quotas and protective tariffs, then of course we lose any influence we have in promoting the expansion of trade. Other nations will begin to do the same thing.
I think the United States today is at her period of great decision in that respect. The United States today has assumed political world leadership, but she must assume economic leadership if she is going to carry through to success the political leadership she has assumed. About 100 years ago Great Britain realized that, as the great commercial centre of the world, she had to open her markets and throw down her tariff barriers. By that move Great Britain became tremendously prosperous. She also gave leadership to a great expansion of prosperity in the whole world. The United States is much greater and more powerful today than the Britain of 100 years ago. It seems to me that although there would be some dislocation, the United States could follow the policy that Great Britain followed 100 years ago.
This would stimulate the development of all countries of the world. It would allay much of the fear that exists today; because many people, even today, who have access to United States markets fear to rely on them too much, because they do not know when the United States may change their policy and plunge them into chaos in their trade relationships. If the United States could make up her mind that she was definitely going to follow the policy which her great President today is asking her to follow, namely to enable nations to expand their trade with her, to buy her production with their production, it would start the world on the road toward greater prosperity, and would ensure that we would not embark on the policy on which the nations of the world embarked in the 1930's.

The Address-Mr. Tucker
When I see the world today, ten years more or less after the end of a great war, reaching about the same stage we reached about ten years after the first war, with the dislocations that follow a war, the getting on their feet of various nations, the pressures beginning to build up through unemployment developing in various nations, pressure upon their governments to put on tariffs or trade quotas or in some way to interfere with trade; when I see that situation developing in various parts of the world today, I wonder if mankind must go through what they went through when they followed a policy of economic nationalism ten years after the end of the first war. We are just reaching that stage today. I hope the great leader of the world today, the United States, will be given the vision and wisdom not to begin to tread the road that was trodden in the 1930's, with all that will result therefrom.
One of the things I hold much to the credit of the present government is that they have steadfastly held to that course of promoting trade, in spite of pressure not only from outside their own ranks but from within; and they are going to have more pressure put upon them. I say this. If the Canadian government wavers in its devotion to that policy of trying to promote freedom and expansion of trade, then they might actually tip the scales when a real fight in that regard is coming to a decision in the United States.
Who can say to what extent the government of Canada, by adhering to the policies and the principles which all governments should have learned from the experience of the 1930's, may influence others? If the government adheres, as it has in the past, to the right policies, who can say to what extent she may have a decisive effect upon the decisions made in the United States and ultimately upon the whole course of world events? If they make a mistake or listen to some of the pleas to interfere with trade, others will do the same thing, and the whole sad story will start all over again.
I want to say to the government that I appreciate the way they have handled the situation thus far. For that reason alone it seems to me that they deserve the support and the approbation of this house and of the country.
I should like to say a few words with regard to the development of this country. At a time like this there is bound to be a measure of readjustment leading to a certain amount of unemployment. There is bound to be difficulty with regard to trade. But the question is this. Has the situation worked out in this country as well as or better than it has worked out in any other country in the


world? We are looking to the United States as an example of what can be done in the way of great development, but what is the record of Canada under the leadership of the present government? Our total gross national product in 1937 was something over $5 billion. In 1954 it had risen to $24 billion, an increase of almost 400 per cent. We think of the United States as going ahead by leaps and bounds with regard to population. But what is the great record of our own country? Since 1945 Canada has increased in population by 19 per cent while the United States has increased by only 12 per cent. Is that not something of which Canadians should be really proud?
During that period we had one of the unique experiences in modern times, that of a great free people deciding by vote to throw in their lot with us. Certainly that is a great achievement of the government of Canada, in that they were able so to conduct the affairs of this country in the previous 15 years that when the time came for Newfoundland to decide whether she would complete confederation, she felt that our country had showed that it was in such good hands, had such good fiscal, economic and other policies and standards, that she could safely join her lot with ours. It seems to me that is something of which the Canadian people may well be proud. They have joined us not by reason of force or pressure exerted on them, but by deciding that they should join their forces with ours. It seems to me that fact speaks volumes for the sort of government our country has enjoyed during the last 15 or 20 years.
If you wish to refer to the rise in the actual standard of living in Canada, you will find that it rose by 13-3 per cent from 1945 to 1952. In the United States during the same period the rise was 15-4 per cent, or a little more than ours. As to the gross national expenditure, or the proportion of it spent on capital development-and we sometimes think Canadians do not spend enough of their savings in developing their own country-in 1952 the proportion in Canada was 18 per cent, and in the United States it was only 14 per cent. The confidence that ordinary Canadians had in the soundness of the future of Canada was marked by the fact that they were willing to invest almost $1 out of every $5 in the development of Canada. That is one of the reasons we have forged ahead as we have.
During that time, under the leadership of the present government, we as a country have not forgotten the weaker members of society, as is shown by the various social welfare measures that have been enacted. Of

measures taken, undoubtedly one of the most important was the one making it possible for the provinces to carry out their constitutional obligations. There is no use in a province having certain powers if it has not the financial means of exercising those powers. A province like Saskatchewan could not possibly give the standard of education, the standard of health, or the standard of roads that could be given by a province like Ontario, with means of reaching the great sources of wealth in the great corporations in that province. With our own provincial resources alone we could not possibly establish, with regard to education and health, a standard of citizenship that could compare with that which could be established in Ontario.
This government recognized that there could not be first-class and second-class citizens in Canada, that all provinces had to be given the means of providing a minimum standard of education, a minimum standard of health and a minimum standard of the other things that the provinces should supply. So they embarked upon these financial agreements.
These agreements mean a great deal to the province of Saskatchewan. Of the money spent by the government of Saskatchewan about 40 cents out of every dollar comes from the federal treasury, and there is no doubt that Saskatchewan could not maintain some of the programs of which it is so proud if it were not for these financial agreements.

In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I would draw particularly the attention of the people who have been finding so much fault with the province of Quebec to something that should never be forgotten. If our compatriots of French-speaking origin had not been willing to join in bringing about confederation, if they had not been willing to trust their fellow citizens of English-speaking origin, confederation would not have been possible. I say it ill behooves any member of the C.C.F. party, whose only provincial government in Canada depends almost for its very existence upon the continuation of these agreements, to find fault with our leader for going to Quebec and trying to work out an arrangement whereby Quebec will come into this scheme and be satisfied with it. It is only on that basis, Mr. Speaker, that we can be sure these financial agreements are a part of our confederation set-up; and the present Prime Minister, in going as far as he could to try to work out some satisfactory arrangement with Quebec, has helped to complete that foundation.
I say that far from the people of Canada being humiliated, as was said by a member of the C.C.F. party in the house, by the Prime Minister going to meet the premier of Quebec to try to work out some sort of satisfactory arrangement that would give them a chance to share in this program together with the rest of Canada, the people of Canada will honour, as I do, that willingness to serve which does not stand upon false dignity but goes out to try to do the best it can for the country. Surely that is in keeping with the teaching in which we nearly all believe; he who would be a leader amongst you, let him be the greatest servant of all. Is it not something that we have a prime minister who, when he sees a chance to get this matter settled in the interests of Canada, says, "Certainly I will go and meet you and talk with you."
I know that the socialists, particularly the socialist leaders in Great Britain, have praised Winston Churchill because he has said that in order to try to promote the peace of the world he will go any place and meet anybody. Yet they find fault with our Prime Minister because he is willing to go to meet a fellow Canadian to work out a common Canadian problem.


There were two items in the speech from the throne with which I was very pleased indeed; because after all, as has been pointed out, the Liberal party step by step has brought in a program cf social welfare that is not excelled by any country in the world. The standard of living of the average individual in Canada is just as high as in any country in the world. The standard of living of the older people, the people who need help from the state, is not excelled in any country in the world. This has been brought about step by step by various measures as the people have been willing and able to pay for them.
One such measure that will be brought into effect during this session is the provision of pensions for the needy, totally disabled. I think every member of the house will be pleased to vote for that, and I would be very surprised if the Social Credit group voted against it for fear of it being branded as a socialist measure.
Of course I do not accept the argument of the hon. member for Macleod for a single moment. I suggest that it is basic Liberal policy to promote social welfare. As you promote development and expand your national income by a system of controlled free enterprise, there is more chance of doing something for the needy and helpless than by hampering development by attempting to get the utmost out of what might be regarded as equitable distribution. Surely we can do more by increasing our gross national product from $5 billion to $24 billion; surely we can do more for the old, the unemployed, the helpless and the blind by such an increase in our gross national product than we can by any system of very refined distribution. As I see it, that is the answer of the Liberal party to socialism. It hampers development which is the basis upon which one can really improve the lot of the needy by concentrating too much on distribution. Another measure about which I was very pleased to see a reference was the proposal to improve the position of those receiving the war veterans allowance
Before I conclude, however, I should like to deal with a problem facing western Canada today. As you know, in 1939 the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was passed under which the farmer contributes one per cent of the receipts from the sale of his grain. This is collected by the federal government. In the case of crop failure, payments are made to the farmers.
At the time that act was passed the farmer received about 57 cents per bushel for his wheat, on an average. The levy of 1 per cent meant that the federal government collected about half a cent per bushel. For

the last eight years the federal government has been collecting, under this 1 per cent provision, 1 [DOT] 6 cents per bushel on an average price prevailing during that time of $1.63. This is almost three times as much as it had been collecting when the act was passed.
The difficulty is that the payments to the farmers remain practically as they were when the act was passed, with the maximum payment being $500. Today $500 will not go even half as far as it would when the act was first passed. This payment was supposed to enable the farmer to put in his crop and tide himself over to the following year. It was not too generous an allowance to do that. Today, when the dollar does not go nearly as far, of course this payment does not do what the act was originally designed to accomplish.
The actual costs the farmers must pay to live and carry on their occupation have risen to an extent indicated by the fact that taking the index for the base period 1935-1939 as 100, the figure today is 225. In other words, it takes $225 today to do the work that $100 would have done in the period 1935-1939. Today, therefore, $500 will not do as much as $250 would do when the act was first passed.
Here is the situation. For the last eight years the government has been collecting almost three times as much per bushel as when the act was passed, and when a crop failure comes along, as it did last year, the farmer receives in actual purchasing power less than half as much to tide him over until the next year.

So far as the cheaper dollar is concerned, if you people could have put your policy into effect the dollar would not be worth half what it is today.
The fact that the dollar will not go as far as it would 10 or 15 years ago has been recognized in other fields. Superannuation rates have been increased. Old age pensions have been doubled compared to what they were when first introduced. Pensions for war veterans have been doubled. The salaries of civil servants, I believe, have been more than doubled. When I first sat in this house members of parliament drew $3,600, and their salaries have been substantially increased. The Address-Mr. Tucker
The farmer says that when he has been paying into this fund for some time on the basis of an undepreciated dollar, under an act designed to carry him over in the event of crop failure, then he should have the same recognition that has been given to these other groups. This provision is something in the nature of unemployment insurance. The farmer believes this was a good act, and if it is going to do the thing it should do then he should be given the same purchasing power as envisaged by the act when it was first passed.
I am quite aware of the fact that the federal government has to put money into this scheme. Up to last fall they had paid out $144 million and collected from the farmers only $73 million. In other words they paid out almost $2 for every dollar collected. Somebody may ask, in view of this, why I am suggesting the payments ought to be increased. At the time the act was passed it was recognized that you could not have an actuarially sound scheme of this sort that would carry itself. The government deemed it wise to have a plan whereby, in the event of crop failure, the farmers could get some money to carry them over until next year out of a fund to which they had contributed, rather than have the government pay out money from public funds entirely by way of relief or agricultural assistance. Today I believe it is generally recognized as being much sounder to have a scheme whereby people contribute to a fund, rather than have the whole burden fall upon the national treasury.
This was a good act when passed. I suggest now that the payments be increased so that they will have the same value in tiding the farmer over as they had when the act was first passed. I am also aware of the fact that somebody may say, well, you are doing that only for the prairie farmers. I suggest that if the farmers in any other branch of agriculture are willing to contribute to such a scheme, it would be a good thing to give them the same protection as the prairie farmer receives. I feel that in every way that would be better than waiting until disaster strikes and having these people have to come to ask for something by way of agricultural assistance.
I feel that would be fairer to agriculture; because we recognize that agriculture, and particularly western agriculture, suffers from protective tariffs more than other industries. Some of the protected industries can look after themselves in the case of set-backs. Farmers, and particularly the prairie farmers, have never been in that position, except for

The Address-Mr. Bryce a few fortunate ones. It was recognized, therefore, that they should receive some protection like this as some compensation.
I would appeal to the government to give consideration at this time to increasing the payments under the Prairie Farm-Assistance Act, especially since many of our farmers have had almost complete crop failures. This would not result in a loss to the economy as a whole, because over and over again it has been demonstrated that if you destroy the purchasing power of the farmers, particularly the western farmers, you begin to add to the lines of the unemployed in the rest of Canada.
The act is a splendid one, one of the finest ever passed. This is one way in which we could put that act, passed by a Liberal government in 1939, in a position to do the job it was able to do when it was first passed. We would merely be recognizing the change in the value of money. I make this suggestion in the hope that the government will recognize its merit, as it has so properly done in the many other fields I have mentioned.

In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I am taking it for granted that the leader of this group congratulated the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address, so I shall not need to do it. I will say to the two new members that I hope their sojourn in the House of Commons will be as pleasant as mine has been over the years.
Now, I do not want to rehash the Selkirk by-election in any way, but I owe thanks to some people, for they certainly helped me in that by-election. My friend the genial Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) spent some pleasant but ineffective days in the constituency. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) found his mission equally fruitless. My good friend the parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister certainly created some heat, but no light. Since the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) appeared only for a one-day stand, I accepted that as a polite tribute to a lost cause. I appreciated the interest shown by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), but it is obvious that the statements made by these gentlemen carried no weight. Indeed, as I said earlier, they were of great assistance to me in winning the seat and therefore I do appreciate the co-operation they gave.
Many veterans' organizations, and others, have written me and come to see me personally making representations with respect to war veterans allowances. I feel I would be failing in my duty if I did not bring this

matter again to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe). These groups have requested me to draw the attention of the minister to the plight of the many veterans receiving benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
However, since the beginning of this session the minister has placed a resolution on the order paper to deal with this problem. The different veterans' organizations are pretty well agreed on what they want for the veterans who have become old before their time. In many cases they are broken in health. These organizations ask that the allowance be raised to $60 for a single person and $120 for a married person, per month. Permissible income has been a serious complaint, and they ask that it be raised to $1,200 for a single man and $2,000 for a married man. I am pleased to note that the matter will be discussed this session, and I hope the minister will meet their demands.
The old age pensioner is still receiving $40 a month, and the pensioner between the ages of 65 and 69 is still subject to the means test. Surely we can find ways and means to increase this amount. Every day we read about some group or other getting an increase in salary, and many of those people are not in the low-income brackets. It has been announced that a bill will be introduced to increase judges' salaries, and other increases are going to be asked. Anyone who will look at the order paper can see them there.
In the recent by-election I visited many elderly people, a good many of whom were finding it hard to get along on $40 a month. About a month ago Val Werier, writing in the Winnipeg Tribune, disclosed some alarming facts concerning the living conditions of elderly citizens in Winnipeg. Not only is this happening in Winnipeg, but it is also found in other cities, in fact right across Canada. I have clipped from the Montreal Gazette, a city far removed from Winnipeg, which is as follows:
An 80-year old woman found near death from malnutrition in a shabby one-room apartment on Aylmer street, is slowly being nursed back to health in St. Mary's hospital.
Weakened by a diet that afforded her no more than tea and toast, the woman was taken to hospital in an ambulance. She had lived in the apartment since her husband died of cancer six years ago. But of her $40 old age pension each month, $35 was taken to pay the rent. The remainder, $5, bought a month's supply of food.
That is a deplorable condition for such a fine country as this, and we should be able to do something to relieve it. I know the general opinion on the government side is that we cannot afford an increase at this time. But I have lived through three wars- the South African war, world war I and

world war II-and I know we were always hard up before those wars. No one had any money; but when war was declared we could find all kinds of money.
A former minister of finance-I believe it was Mr. Dunning-when he sat over where our Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) now sits was asked by one of the members of this group to set aside some money for unemployment relief early in 1939. What did he reply? He said, "Does my young friend think that money grows on gooseberry bushes?" But remember this; that when war was declared in 1939 the government found the gooseberry bushes. They found the money to buy armaments.
Our old age citizens are far more important than armaments. Perhaps I do not need to tell the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the plight of the interlake farmers at the present time. He was out there, and I know from past experience that when he goes anywhere he looks into things like this. I give him credit for that. It would have pleased me even more if it had been possible for the minister, when visiting the constituency of Selkirk, to go back 60 or 70 miles farther north to see conditions there. I know the Minister of Justice knows the district very well, because he spent many years up there, in one way or another.

There is one other thing I would ask the minister to do, and that is to give serious consideration to the establishment of a national livestock marketing board. Such a board should have been established a long

time ago, and I believe the farmers of this country are beginning to realize that we must have it. What has taken place within the livestock industry over the past two years is nothing short of a tragedy, because there has been a 50 per cent drop over that period. But the farmers' costs have not dropped. The average price of beef cattle going through the Winnipeg market this year is around $130, but three years ago the average price was $260. It will therefore be seen that the price of beef cattle has been reduced by 50 per cent over the past two years.
On the other hand we find that over-all production costs increased by 8 per cent over the same period, thereby constituting a total loss to the farmer of almost 60 per cent. The latest available information indicates that the situation might become even worse. I fail to see any reasonable justification for the drastic reduction in the price of beef to the producer. Certainly it cannot be argued that such a slump in producers' prices can be attributed to any oversupply or surplus, because we had only 5 per cent over and above our needs, and only 5 per cent was exported. The September 1953 issue of the current review of agricultural conditions states that the Canadian people consumed 95 per cent of the total amount marketed, and only 5 per cent was exported during the first seven months of 1953.
Those figures show that we are not producing more than we can dispose of, and should prove beyond the shadow of a doubt that there is no possible reason for the decline in livestock prices. If supply and demand have something to do with prices, as we are constantly led to believe, then the price of beef cattle should be increasing instead of going down because livestock production is constantly decreasing in direct ratio to the increase in population. At the beginning of the century the cattle population was 1,200 per 1,000 inhabitants. In 1954 it was only about 750. Our cattle population is therefore decreasing, and as long as the present system of marketing livestock is continued the producer will inevitably receive inadequate returns from the sale of his products.

Mr. Speaker, differences of opinion
have been and still are one of the sacred rights of democracy. This is especially true in a deliberative assembly such as this. During the present debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne hon. members have fully exercised their right to differ.
I do not intend to add much to what has already been said during the course of this debate, but I feel it is my duty to submit some of the views shared by my constituents in Glengarry-Prescott, with particular reference to the speech from the throne. But may I first be permitted to sincerely congratulate the hon. members for Verdun (Mr. Leduc) and Toronto Trinity (Mr. Carrick) on the magnificent oratory they demonstrated in proposing and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sure that they both expressed the thoughts of the Canadian people at large.
We all noticed that, while dealing mainly with general policy, the speech from the throne made clear the constant care of the government for the betterment of the welfare of the Canadian people, through a policy based on social security and economic stabilization in our country as well as in the rest of the world.
Once again the government is showing its broadmindedness in bringing this house and the people of Canada at large to consider the problem presented by the frame of a universal community growing smaller every day. Unfortunately Canada, as a growing nation, has not yet the facilities with which to measure itself with many of its elders in the cultural field. That is why I feel justified in deploring the fact that the government is not yet ready to implement the recommendations of the royal commission on arts, letters and sciences. The proposed establishment of a council on arts, letters and sciences is of great interest to the youth of Canada in general and, as I see it, is a logical evolution toward a federal department of youth.
Solving the immediate problems and needs is evidently one of the main things the government must keep in mind in laying down their policies. But one must not forget that we are now working for the future, actually for the generation which will be called to lead the nation tomorrow. I know

The Address-Mr. Bruneau it is the intention of the government eventually to create such a council and such a department, but I sincerely believe that each day and each month that such a move is postponed is a delay in allowing our young people to develop their talents in a way to enable them better to serve a better Canada.
As much as my constituents are aware of the necessity of furthering the cultural and physical development of the younger generations, they are also quite appreciative of the laws introduced to improve conditions among the farm and industrial workers. As you know, Glengarry-Prescott is of dual composition not only in name but also in the activities of its population. Farming and industry are its two components, and both these groups looked at the speech from the throne with a mixture of satisfaction and anxiety.
The majority in Glengarry-Prescott is made up of people of the agricultural class, and my constituency now ranks among the largest cheese producing constituencies in the world. Our dairy farm owners, I am sorry to say, were greatly disappointed over the absence from the speech from the throne of any mention of added help to solve the acute problems faced by them. But they are even more worried over the importation into Canada of some 2J million pounds of New Zealand cheese. With the millions of pounds of Canadian cheddar cheese at present in storage, the people I represent in this house are at a loss to understand why such authorization was granted.
Eastern Ontario-and for that matter a good part of eastern Canada-is aware of the difficulties our cheese producers have gone through during the last two or three years, with regard to the marketing of their product. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we had to go through a great many interviews in order to secure a reasonable price for that commodity. Now every spring the farmers of my constituency and in that region are in anguish and doubt as to the price that will be secured through the marketing of their product. I should like to see this government place this commodity under import control while we have a surplus on hand. I hope we shall see to it that this New Zealand cheese does not add to the already heavy burden on our local farmers.
That two-way trade should be promoted to ensure markets for Canada is an already accepted theory. But that this practice should be implemented particularly by means of one of the products which we have in surplus is something that is not as easily understood. If it is necessary to accept this importation of New Zealand cheese in order to maintain the balance of trade between our country and New Zealand, may I suggest that we could
fMr. Bruneau.]
possibly exchange part of our surplus cheese or the whole of the imported cheese under our Colombo assistance, for example. It would be a way of counteracting the bad effects of such an importation, and would also be a way of relieving our dairy producers of their annual fear with regard to the marketing of their product. At this point may I also suggest that federal subsidies would be especially welcomed by the hard-pressed cheese producing industry, and that they would also help to maintain the stability of our national economy as a whole.
As regards help to certain groups of the population, in the speech from the throne I notice that it is the intention of the government to provide facilities for loans to fishermen similar to those provided to farmers by the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This is a commendable move, but the farmers would also appreciate it if the facilities extended to them by the above-mentioned act were increased in such a way that they could benefit from higher loans at a lower rate of interest. At present it is felt that the conditions laid down for the securing of a loan are altogether too hard to be met by the average farmer, and that in most cases the obtainable loans are not sufficient for the purposes to be served. By reconsidering the amount and the interest rates with regard to loans to farmers, I am sure the government would not only greatly help the farming industry but would also help itself.
Mr. Speaker, I have taken this opportunity to stress a few of the problems of the cheese producing and farming industries, for two main reasons. The first is that I am one of those who still believe agriculture to be the most stable element of the Canadian economy. The second one is that I represent a riding made up mainly of people of the agricultural class. Nevertheless, Glengarry-Prescott also has a large portion of its population directly engaged in industry. That being so, they are fully aware of the fact that employment is of paramount importance at the present time.
I was also glad to see that one of the highlights of the speech from the throne was aimed at providing more employment through a new scheme of federal public works. It is agreed that the present unemployment is seasonal and temporary, but I feel that the government were well advised in laying down a program to relieve the tension voiced from certain quarters.

On the other hand, convinced that their municipality could provide a logical site, the people of that region rejoice at a recent opinion that Canada has now reached a point where heavy industry should be decentralized. Geographically and ethnographically we enjoy' first-class industrial activity, but there is room for more factories. Allow me also to inform you, sir, that our working hands are "tops". I and my constituents feel that such a policy of industrial redistri-
The Address-Mr. Bruneau bution cannot be successfully achieved with these thriving municipalities left out of the picture.
I am well aware of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that important measures announced in the speech from the throne have to be studied with diligence and voted upon. Finally may I say that the speech from the throne offers a rather substantial program of measures, and I believe it should give the average man the feeling that Canada is really going forward under a progressive and competent government.
